# FAQ (/docs/guide/faq)





<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="How is DiaX different from React Flow?">
    React Flow is a full-featured interactive graph UI library built for drag-and-drop node editors, visual programming tools, and interactive workflows.

    DiaX is a **headless diagram-as-code engine** with no core runtime dependencies, designed for static, declarative diagrams. DiaX uses CSS Grid for layout instead of absolute positioning, making it SSR-friendly and naturally responsive.

    |                   | DiaX                       | React Flow                         |
    | ----------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
    | Bundle checks     | Tracked in this repository | See React Flow's published package |
    | Core dependencies | 0                          | See React Flow's published package |
    | Interaction       | Static (by design)         | Drag/pan/zoom                      |
    | Layout            | CSS Grid (auto)            | Manual positioning                 |
    | Use case          | Documentation, AI output   | Visual editors                     |

    If you need users to drag nodes around, use React Flow. If you need diagrams rendered from data or code, use DiaX.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How is DiaX different from Mermaid?">
    Mermaid turns a portable text DSL into an SVG using its own renderer and theme system. It is usually
    the better fit when text portability and broad diagram-family coverage matter most.

    DiaX keeps nodes as **real DOM elements** while drawing connections in an SVG overlay. It is aimed at
    cases where nodes must contain application components or follow an existing CSS design system.

    |               | DiaX                                               | Mermaid                                    |
    | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
    | Output        | DOM nodes (JSX)                                    | SVG                                        |
    | Styling       | Application CSS/Tailwind for DOM nodes             | Mermaid themes, config and SVG/CSS styling |
    | Custom nodes  | Application components through framework renderers | Mermaid syntax and renderer extensions     |
    | Bundle checks | Tracked in this repository                         | See Mermaid's published package            |
    | Input format  | JSON / JSX / DSL                                   | Mermaid DSL                                |

    `parseMermaid()` from `@diax/mermaid` imports a documented subset of six Mermaid diagram families
    into a normalized DiaX AST. It is a migration and composition path, not full Mermaid compatibility;
    unsupported families or syntax return diagnostics.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How is DiaX different from D2?">
    D2 is a standalone diagram scripting language and CLI tool. It compiles `.d2` files into SVG/PNG images. It runs as a binary (Go), not in the browser.

    DiaX is a **JavaScript library** you import into your app. It runs in the browser (or on the server via SSR) and produces live DOM elements, not static images.

    |             | DiaX                               | D2              |
    | ----------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------- |
    | Runtime     | Browser / Node.js                  | CLI binary      |
    | Output      | Live DOM                           | SVG/PNG files   |
    | Integration | npm package                        | Standalone tool |
    | Frameworks  | React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Vanilla | N/A             |

    If you need diagrams embedded in a web app, use DiaX. If you need standalone diagram files for documentation pipelines, D2 is a great choice.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does DiaX work with SSR?">
    Partially, with a clear client boundary. DiaX can render the node content, topology-derived CSS Grid
    placement and a stable empty edge shell on the server.

    Pixel-accurate SVG paths require DOM measurements and complete after hydration. Font, image or
    content-size changes may still move nodes, so applications should use stable sizing and test their
    own loading states instead of assuming zero layout shift.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use DiaX commercially?">
    Yes. DiaX is **MIT licensed** — free for personal, commercial, and enterprise use. No attribution required (though appreciated).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What's the bundle size?">
    The core engine (`diax`) has no runtime dependencies. Package size changes are measured by the repository's size-limit configuration instead of duplicated as a number in the docs, so the result stays tied to the actual build artifact. Run `pnpm size:check` from the repository root for the current measurement.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which frameworks are supported?">
    DiaX has a framework-agnostic Core and five framework adapter packages:

    * React (`@diax/react`)
    * Vue (`@diax/vue`)
    * Svelte (`@diax/svelte`)
    * Solid (`@diax/solid`)
    * Vanilla JS (`@diax/vanilla`)

    The adapters are currently Alpha and do not yet claim identical rich labels, events, DOM measurement,
    SSR or accessibility behavior. The shared contract matrix, not package count, determines parity.
    Other frameworks can consume Core's pure layout output, but that is not a sixth framework binding.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use custom node components?">
    Yes, in two ways:

    1. **`renderNode` prop** — a function that receives node data and returns JSX:

    ```tsx
    <FlowDiagram
      renderNode={(node, state) => (
        <MyCustomCard title={node.content} highlighted={state === 'highlighted'} />
      )}
    />
    ```

    2. **`nodeTypes` registry** — define renderers by type, then assign types to nodes:

    ```tsx
    <FlowDiagram
      nodes={[
        { id: 'gw', type: 'gateway', content: 'API Gateway' },
        { id: 'svc', type: 'service', content: 'Auth' },
      ]}
      nodeTypes={{
        gateway: (node) => <GatewayCard>{node.content}</GatewayCard>,
        service: (node) => <ServiceCard>{node.content}</ServiceCard>,
      }}
    />
    ```

    Resolution order: `renderNode` > `nodeTypes[node.type]` > default renderer.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does DiaX support animations?">
    Yes. DiaX provides **5 edge animation presets**:

    | Preset              | Effect                         |
    | ------------------- | ------------------------------ |
    | `"flow"`            | Flowing dashes along the edge  |
    | `"pulse"`           | Breathing opacity effect       |
    | `"shimmer"`         | Light traveling along the edge |
    | `"reverse-flow"`    | Reverse flowing dashes         |
    | `"reverse-shimmer"` | Reverse shimmer                |

    ```tsx
    <FlowDiagram
      relations={[
        { from: 'a', to: 'b', animate: 'flow' },
        { from: 'b', to: 'c', animate: 'shimmer' },
      ]}
    />
    ```

    Entrance animations are also supported via the `stagger` prop.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I export diagrams as images?">
    Not through a stable framework export yet. DiaX diagrams combine normal DOM content with an SVG
    edge overlay, so an edge-only SVG export is not the complete result. Wrap the diagram in an element
    you own and use a DOM-capture library at the application boundary, with explicit font, asset,
    background and browser tests. Notebook has an internal export adapter, but it is not exported by
    `@diax/react`, `@diax/vue` or the other framework packages.
  </Accordion>
</Accordions>


# Framework Parity Matrix (/docs/guide/feature-parity)



Same semantics, native composition [#same-semantics-native-composition]

All five adapters can render the same Diagram Definition. React, Vue, Solid and Svelte expose
`FlowDiagram` and `Mindmap` components; Vanilla uses the imperative `createDiagram()` interface.
They share layout semantics and runtime behavior, but they should not imitate one another's
composition syntax. A missing React-shaped prop is not automatically a missing capability.

The table below reports the current runtime surface. Its values are locked to the repository's
internal `docs/adapter-capabilities.json` manifest so documentation changes cannot silently outrun
the tested adapter surface. `⚠` means the underlying Core capability exists, but the high-level
adapter does not provide the complete lifecycle or convenience contract.

{/* adapter-capabilities:start */}

| Capability                           |          React          |          Vue          |        Solid       |         Svelte         |      Vanilla      |
| ------------------------------------ | :---------------------: | :-------------------: | :----------------: | :--------------------: | :---------------: |
| Automatic Flow / Mindmap             |       ✅ Components      |      ✅ Components     |    ✅ Components    |      ✅ Components      | ✅ `createDiagram` |
| Headless binding interface           |          ✅ Hook         |      ✅ Composable     |      ✅ Signals     | ✅ `createDiagramStore` | ⚠ use `diax` Core |
| High-level reactive update lifecycle |            ✅            |           ✅           |          ✅         |    ✅ Component props   |    ✅ `update()`   |
| Custom node renderer                 |      ✅ `renderNode`     |     ✅ scoped slot     |   ✅ `renderNode`   |       ✅ node slot      |   ✅ `renderNode`  |
| `nodeTypes` registry                 |            ✅            |           ✅           |          ✅         |            —           |         ✅         |
| String edge labels                   |            ✅            |           ✅           |          ✅         |            ✅           |         ✅         |
| Framework-native rich edge label     |       ✅ React node      |     ✅ scoped slot     |  ✅ render function |      ✅ named slot      |   ✅ DOM callback  |
| Framework-native rich group label    |       ✅ React node      |     ✅ scoped slot     |     ✅ Solid JSX    |      ✅ named slot      |   ✅ DOM callback  |
| Label-aware node clearance           |            ✅            |           ✅           |          ✅         |            ✅           |         ✅         |
| Hover path highlighting              |            ✅            |           ✅           |          ✅         |            ✅           |         ✅         |
| Interactive edge events              |            ✅            |           ✅           |          ✅         |            ✅           |         ✅         |
| Nested group boundaries              |            ✅            |           ✅           |          ✅         |            ✅           |         ✅         |
| High-level namespace isolation       |            ✅            |           ✅           |          ✅         |            ✅           |         ✅         |
| SSR shell and hydration              |  ✅ SSR shell + hydrate  | ✅ SSR shell + hydrate | ✅ built conditions |  ✅ Vite SSR + hydrate  |         —         |
| JSX Definition Adapter               |   ✅ `@diax/react/jsx`   |           —           |          —         |            —           |         —         |
| Connect authored DOM                 | ✅ `@diax/react/connect` |           —           |          —         |            —           |         —         |

{/* adapter-capabilities:end */}

`—` means the adapter does not expose that interface today. It does not imply that the Core engine
or relation model lacks the underlying capability.

Required parity: runtime contract [#required-parity-runtime-contract]

Every stable official adapter must eventually satisfy the same behavioral contract for:

* relation parsing and graph validation;
* Flow and Mindmap placement;
* anchors, paths and markers;
* DOM measurement and stable target identity;
* semantic group validation, nested placement, and derived boundary bindings;
* highlight semantics and accessible edge interaction;
* prop/input updates without losing authored DOM state;
* observer cleanup, SSR safety, and hydration stability;
* intrinsic edge-label measurement and automatic node clearance when Diagram owns layout;
* theme values from `diax/themes`.

These are product guarantees, not optional syntax sugar. The release browser contract covers built
package output for React, Vue, Solid, Svelte and Vanilla in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, while
framework pages document adapter-specific SSR and composition rules.

The SSR row describes adapter-level evidence, not every meta-framework. Next RSC and the
`remark-diax` Fumadocs pipeline have dedicated production fixtures. Nuxt, SolidStart, SvelteKit,
Next MDX and Docusaurus remain host-specific follow-up work even where the underlying Vue, Solid,
Svelte or React adapter already has an SSR shell and hydration contract.

All five adapters preserve stable label identity, feed per-label measurements into the shared
routing plan, and reserve the largest intrinsic label on the primary Grid axis. The feedback remains
private adapter lifecycle behavior; users do not provide dimensions or manually refresh Diagram.

Idiomatic convenience: same capability, native syntax [#idiomatic-convenience-same-capability-native-syntax]

DOM presentation seams should follow each framework rather than share one artificial prop shape:

| Need            | Idiomatic interface                                                 |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| React content   | JSX / React nodes and render functions                              |
| Vue content     | Scoped slots and VNodes                                             |
| Solid content   | Accessor-preserving render functions                                |
| Svelte content  | Slots today; typed snippets when the support floor permits Svelte 5 |
| Vanilla content | DOM callbacks receiving an owned element                            |

Rich edge and group labels belong in this tier because DOM-native presentation is a core DiaX
value. Edge labels use a Vue `#edge-label` slot, a Solid render function, a Svelte named slot and a
Vanilla DOM callback. Group labels use the corresponding native presentation seam while keeping
derived boundary geometry private. The shared meaning matches while the syntax remains native.
Typed Svelte snippets can replace the legacy slot surface only when the support floor permits a
Svelte 5-only interface.

`nodeTypes` is useful when application or AI-authored `node.type` values map to a trusted design
system registry. Svelte's node slot already supports an idiomatic component map, so DiaX should not
add a React-shaped registry merely to turn one table cell green.

Framework-specific authoring leaves [#framework-specific-authoring-leaves]

React-only authoring leaves [#react-only-authoring-leaves]

JSX Definition and Connect accept framework-native React content, so they live in isolated React
subpaths rather than Core or every adapter. Diagram-only users do not load either optional runtime.

Other adapters may gain their own authoring leaves only where their ecosystem provides a genuinely
better interface—for example Vue directives, Solid directives, or Svelte actions for connecting
already-authored DOM. They should first prove a real user workflow and a second adapter seam; they
must not be mechanical ports of React JSX components.

Node presentation [#node-presentation]

Vue and Svelte use slots, Solid uses functions returning Solid JSX, and Vanilla renders into a real
element passed to a callback. These adapters share the semantic node and relation model without
pretending framework composition is identical.

Naming and reactivity [#naming-and-reactivity]

Parity does not require every reactive primitive to be named `useDiagram`. React hooks and Vue
composables make that name natural; Solid primitives generally use `create*`, and Svelte uses
`createDiagramStore`. The store exposes `updateOptions()` for explicit topology and layout updates;
the former `useDiagram` spelling remains a deprecated compatibility alias during Alpha.

Generics [#generics]

The low-level Core, hooks, composables, stores and Vanilla interface independently preserve node
content, edge labels, and group labels in the order `<NodeContent, EdgeLabel, GroupLabel>`.
High-level components constrain content to values their framework renderer can safely display; check
the adapter's Props page before designing a cross-framework component library.

Maturity [#maturity]

The adapters remain Alpha. “Official” means they are maintained and release-tested in this
repository; it does not promise identical ecosystem integrations or authoring syntax.

The next adapter work is ordered by user-visible leverage:

1. complete Safari + VoiceOver, Edge + NVDA and real Windows High Contrast hardware acceptance;
2. evaluate a second Connect-style adapter only from a real Vue, Solid or Svelte authored-DOM case;
3. add framework-specific authoring leaves only after a real adopter proves the seam.

The maintenance rationale and package deletion-test results are recorded in the
[Owner package and interface audit](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/blob/main/docs/owner/2026-07-package-capability-interface-audit.md).

<Cards>
  <Card title="React" href="/docs/react" description="Diagram, JSX Definition and Connect" />

  <Card title="Vue" href="/docs/vue" description="Components, slots and composables" />

  <Card title="Svelte" href="/docs/svelte" description="Components, slots and stores" />

  <Card title="Solid" href="/docs/solid" description="Components, render functions and signals" />

  <Card title="Vanilla" href="/docs/vanilla" description="Imperative DOM lifecycle" />
</Cards>


# Getting Started (/docs/guide)





Start from the job [#start-from-the-job]

DiaX is a DOM-native diagram runtime. Your content remains real HTML and framework components;
DiaX supplies automatic placement or connection geometry at an explicit ownership seam.

<Callout type="info">
  **DiaX connects real DOM. You explicitly choose who owns layout.**
</Callout>

| What you already have                                   | Start with               | Layout owner                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Nodes and relations                                     | **Diagram**              | DiaX places nodes and routes edges                                          |
| JSX, Tailwind or semantic HTML with the right placement | **Connect DOM**          | Your CSS places content; DiaX connects it                                   |
| Mermaid source                                          | **Mermaid Import**       | Mermaid supplies topology; DiaX renders the supported subset as DOM         |
| Markdown or MDX fences in a build pipeline              | **MDX Integration**      | Remark transforms supported source and reports invalid fences through VFile |
| AI-generated content                                    | **Agent-first Workflow** | Choose Diagram JSON or reviewed Connect JSX, then validate the built result |
| A topology but no visual design system                  | **UI Primitives**        | DiaX places styled DOM presentation primitives                              |

<Cards>
  <Card title="Diagram" href="/docs/react" description="Render nodes and relations with automatic layout" />

  <Card title="Connect DOM" href="/docs/react/connect" description="Draw relations over existing JSX and responsive CSS" />

  <Card title="Mermaid Import" href="/docs/guide/mermaid" description="Convert supported Mermaid families into real DOM" />

  <Card title="Markdown & MDX" href="/docs/guide/mdx-guide" description="Transform supported fences with build and live-preview diagnostics" />

  <Card title="AI & Agents" href="/docs/guide/agent-workflow" description="Move from a communication question to a validated, built and reviewable artifact" />

  <Card title="UI Primitives" href="/docs/ui-react" description="Use ready-made DOM components for common diagram vocabulary" />
</Cards>

Fastest path: Diagram [#fastest-path-diagram]

Use Diagram when topology is already data and DiaX should place it. Pick your framework, select its
package, and pass `nodes` plus `relations`. During the unpublished preview, the package panel gives
you the repository workflow instead of a registry command that cannot succeed.

<Steps>
  Prepare your framework adapter [#prepare-your-framework-adapter]

  <Tabs groupId="framework" items="['React', 'Vue', 'Solid', 'Svelte', 'Vanilla JS']">
    <Tab value="React">
      <InstallTabs packages="['@diax/react']" description="React bindings (includes the Core engine)" />
    </Tab>

    <Tab value="Vue">
      <InstallTabs packages="['@diax/vue']" description="Vue 3 bindings" />
    </Tab>

    <Tab value="Svelte">
      <InstallTabs packages="['@diax/svelte']" description="Svelte bindings" />
    </Tab>

    <Tab value="Solid">
      <InstallTabs packages="['@diax/solid']" description="SolidJS bindings" />
    </Tab>

    <Tab value="Vanilla JS">
      <InstallTabs packages="['@diax/vanilla']" description="Imperative DOM adapter" />
    </Tab>
  </Tabs>

  Render the same topology [#render-the-same-topology]

  <Tabs groupId="framework" items="['React', 'Vue', 'Solid', 'Svelte', 'Vanilla JS']">
    <Tab value="React">
      ```tsx contract
      import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

      export function CheckoutFlow() {
        return (
          <FlowDiagram
            nodes={[
              { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
              { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
              { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
            ]}
            relations={['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db']}
          />
        );
      }
      ```
    </Tab>

    <Tab value="Vue">
      ```vue contract
      <script setup lang="ts">
      import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/vue';

      const nodes = [
        { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
        { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
        { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
      ];
      const relations = ['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db'];
      </script>

      <template><FlowDiagram :nodes="nodes" :relations="relations" /></template>
      ```
    </Tab>

    <Tab value="Svelte">
      ```svelte contract
      <script lang="ts">
      import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/svelte';

      const nodes = [
        { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
        { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
        { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
      ];
      const relations = ['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db'];
      </script>

      <FlowDiagram {nodes} {relations} />
      ```
    </Tab>

    <Tab value="Solid">
      ```tsx contract solid
      import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/solid';

      export function CheckoutFlow() {
        return (
          <FlowDiagram
            nodes={[
              { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
              { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
              { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
            ]}
            relations={['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db']}
          />
        );
      }
      ```
    </Tab>

    <Tab value="Vanilla JS">
      ```html
      <div id="diagram"></div>
      <script type="module">
        import { createDiagram } from '@diax/vanilla';

        createDiagram(document.querySelector('#diagram'), {
          nodes: [
            { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
            { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
            { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
          ],
          relations: ['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db'],
        });
      </script>
      ```
    </Tab>
  </Tabs>
</Steps>

<DiagramPreview
  title="Expected result"
  code="`<FlowDiagram
nodes={[
  { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
  { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
  { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
]}
relations={['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db']}
/>`"
>
  <FlowDiagram
    nodes="[
    { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
    { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
    { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
  ]"
    relations="['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db']"
  />
</DiagramPreview>

The framework adapter hides parsing, validation, layout, DOM measurement and edge rendering behind
one interface. Move to hooks, stores or Core primitives only when your renderer genuinely needs that
control.

Already own the layout? [#already-own-the-layout]

Do not rebuild a report or dashboard as diagram nodes. Keep the authored DOM and use the isolated
React Connect entry to mark the exact endpoints:

```tsx contract
import { ConnectionSurface, connectionTarget } from '@diax/react/connect';

export function DecisionReport() {
  return (
    <ConnectionSurface relations={[{ from: 'claim', to: 'evidence' }]}>
      <article {...connectionTarget('claim')}>Conversion improved.</article>
      <aside {...connectionTarget('evidence')}>Experiment results</aside>
    </ConnectionSurface>
  );
}
```

[Read the Connect guide →](/docs/react/connect)

Generating with AI? [#generating-with-ai]

Use validated JSON for untrusted runtime output. Use JSX or MDX only in a trusted, reviewed code
workflow. The Agent-first guide connects classification, validation, built preview, review and
delivery without adding a new runtime mode.

[Follow the Agent-first workflow →](/docs/guide/agent-workflow)

Next steps [#next-steps]

# ELK Layout (/docs/guide/layout-elk)



<InstallTabs packages="['@diax/layout-elk']" description="Experimental ELK.js LayoutPlan adapter" />

What ELK adds [#what-elk-adds]

ELK (Eclipse Layout Kernel) is the opt-in engine for graphs that need stronger port ordering,
crossing minimization, orthogonal sections, or non-layered algorithms. DiaX does not bundle ELK into
Core or any framework package.

Use the built-in planner for ordinary layered diagrams: pipelines, architecture overviews, and
small-to-medium DAGs with a readable number of relations per rank transition. Escalate to ELK when
a transition is highly congested, ports need strict ordering, or preserving exact routed sections
matters more than synchronous startup and bundle size.

The recommended API is `computeLayoutPlan()`. It preserves:

* exact pixel node placements and measured node sizes;
* stable source and target ports;
* every ELK edge section and bend point;
* exact label coordinates and measured label sizes;
* native compound-group bounds and absolute descendant positions;
* ordered entry/exit ports where native routes cross semantic group bounds;
* complete plan bounds.

The output is the same engine-neutral `LayoutPlan` used by the built-in planner.

When not to choose ELK [#when-not-to-choose-elk]

Stay with the built-in planner when the graph is an ordinary pipeline, architecture overview or
small-to-medium DAG. ELK adds an asynchronous dependency and a measurement handoff; it does not make
rich DOM content automatically measurable and it does not replace a presentation design system.

Do not choose ELK only because one edge looks imperfect. First confirm that node sizes and edge-label
sizes are measured, the intended layout owner is Diagram rather than Connect, and the graph actually
needs strict port ordering, compound geometry or denser crossing minimization. React can consume an
external `LayoutPlan` today; the other high-level adapters do not yet expose that seam.

<Callout type="warn">
  `@diax/layout-elk` remains experimental. React `DiagramEdges` can consume its plan today. Vue,
  Solid, Svelte, and Vanilla already have per-edge label measurement and incremental route-stability
  parity for their built-in planner, but do not yet expose an external `LayoutPlan` rendering prop.
  A custom compound renderer must place `plan.groups` behind `plan.nodes`; `DiagramEdges` only owns
  edge geometry.
</Callout>

Compound groups [#compound-groups]

Pass the same semantic `groups` used by `FlowDiagram` in the layout context. You still do not author
group coordinates. ELK creates native compound nodes, and `LayoutPlan.groups` retains their final
pixel bounds outermost first. Invalid members, duplicate ownership, or parent cycles fail with the
same structured `DiaxValidationError` diagnostics as the built-in engine.

If a custom ELK renderer places rich group labels on those bounds, pass their measured local boxes
as `groupLabelRects` in `ElkLayoutContext`. DiaX then applies the same border exclusion and group-port
normalization as the built-in planner. Do not estimate label width in the graph definition.

```ts contract
import { elkLayout } from '@diax/layout-elk';
import { parseRelations } from 'diax';

const nodes = [
  { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
  { id: 'api', content: 'API' },
  { id: 'db', content: 'DB' },
];
const groups = [
  { id: 'backend', nodeIds: ['api', 'db'], parentId: 'system' },
  { id: 'system', nodeIds: ['browser'] },
];
const plan = await elkLayout().computeLayoutPlan(
  nodes,
  parseRelations(['browser->api', 'api->db']),
  { groups },
);

plan.groups;
plan.edges.flatMap((edge) => edge.groupPorts ?? []);
```

Use ELK for strict compound geometry or dense cross-group routing. The built-in flow layout keeps
automatic group subtrees in exclusive CSS Grid row bands and derives measured group bounds, which
is sufficient for ordinary architecture and pipeline diagrams.

React: preserve the complete plan [#react-preserve-the-complete-plan]

ELK owns both node placement and routes in this example. The application still owns each node's
actual DOM content.

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="React">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="React">
      React
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>

  <CodeBlockTab value="React">
    ```tsx  title="ElkDiagram.tsx" contract
    import { elkLayout } from '@diax/layout-elk';
    import { DiagramEdges } from '@diax/react';
    import { parseRelations, type LayoutPlan } from 'diax';
    import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

    const nodes = [
      { id: 'gateway', content: 'API Gateway' },
      { id: 'auth', content: 'Auth Service' },
      { id: 'users', content: 'User Service' },
      { id: 'db', content: 'PostgreSQL' },
    ];

    const edges = parseRelations([
      { id: 'gateway-auth', from: 'gateway', to: 'auth', label: 'JWT' },
      { id: 'gateway-users', from: 'gateway', to: 'users', label: 'HTTPS' },
      { id: 'auth-db', from: 'auth', to: 'db', label: 'SQL' },
      { id: 'users-db', from: 'users', to: 'db', label: 'SQL' },
    ]);

    export function ElkDiagram() {
      const [plan, setPlan] = useState<LayoutPlan | null>(null);

      useEffect(() => {
        void elkLayout({ algorithm: 'layered', direction: 'horizontal' })
          .computeLayoutPlan(nodes, edges, {
            nodeSizes: new Map(nodes.map(node => [node.id, { width: 160, height: 56 }])),
            labelSizes: new Map(edges.map(edge => [edge.id!, { width: 64, height: 24 }])),
          })
          .then(setPlan);
      }, []);

      if (!plan) return <p>Computing layout…</p>;
      const content = new Map(nodes.map(node => [node.id, node.content]));

      return (
        <div
          style={{
            position: 'relative',
            width: plan.bounds.width,
            height: plan.bounds.height,
          }}
        >
          {plan.nodes.map(node => (
            <div
              key={node.id}
              data-diax-node={node.id}
              style={{
                position: 'absolute',
                left: node.x,
                top: node.y,
                width: node.width,
                height: node.height,
              }}
            >
              {content.get(node.id)}
            </div>
          ))}
          <DiagramEdges edges={edges} layoutPlan={plan} pathType="orthogonal" />
        </div>
      );
    }
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

Real applications usually measure their node and label components before running ELK. The fixed
sizes above keep the example focused on the adapter contract. Supplying actual sizes is what lets
ELK reserve enough space for rich JSX/Tailwind content.

Invalid geometry fails at the owner [#invalid-geometry-fails-at-the-owner]

ELK is a numeric trust boundary. DiaX validates resolved layout options, consumed node and label
measurements, group-label rectangles, the raw ELK result, and the final engine-neutral plan. A
`NaN`, `Infinity`, or negative extent fails once with `code: "invalid-elk-geometry"` and the exact
path before label, port, crossing, group, or SVG calculations run.

```ts
await elkLayout().computeLayoutPlan(nodes, edges, {
  nodeSizes: new Map([
    ['gateway', { width: Number.NaN, height: 56 }],
  ]),
});
// DiaxElkGeometryError:
// [DiaX: invalid-elk-geometry] context.nodeSizes["gateway"].width ...
```

This adapter-local error is intentionally not another Core diagnostic code or public repair mode.
Fix the owning DOM measurement. Do not replace an invalid value with zero merely to make layout
continue; doing so would turn missing geometry into invented geometry.

Engine-neutral consumption [#engine-neutral-consumption]

Custom renderers can turn a plan into styled SVG path data without depending on React:

```ts contract
import type { LayoutPlan, ParsedRelation } from 'diax';
import { computeEdgePathsFromLayoutPlan } from 'diax/layout-plan';

declare const plan: LayoutPlan;
declare const edges: ParsedRelation[];

const paths = computeEdgePathsFromLayoutPlan(plan, edges, {
  pathType: 'orthogonal',
});
```

`pathType` only selects the visual interpolation of an already planned route. It does not rerun ELK
or replace its sections with a direct Bézier.

Compatibility bridge [#compatibility-bridge]

The original `computeLayout()` method still returns `LayoutResult` for existing integrations:

```ts contract
import { elkLayout } from '@diax/layout-elk';
import { parseRelations } from 'diax';

const nodes = [
  { id: 'a', content: 'A' },
  { id: 'b', content: 'B' },
];
const result = await elkLayout().computeLayout(nodes, parseRelations(['a->b']));
```

<Callout type="warn">
  This bridge quantizes ELK pixels back to DiaX `col`/`row` positions and necessarily discards the
  advanced route geometry. Use it only while migrating an existing `FlowDiagram` integration.
</Callout>

Available algorithms [#available-algorithms]

| Algorithm | Best for                                   |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `layered` | Directed flows and architectures (default) |
| `force`   | Organic network relationships              |
| `stress`  | Distance-preserving graph placement        |
| `mrtree`  | Tree structures                            |
| `radial`  | Center-out structures                      |

All algorithms return the same `LayoutPlan` shape. Algorithm-specific tuning stays inside the
opt-in ELK package; ordinary DiaX users should not need raw ELK option keys.

Related [#related]

* [Graph & Layout Primitives](/docs/reference/graph-layout)
* [Edge Rendering Primitives](/docs/reference/edge-rendering)
* [Layout modes](/docs/guide/layout-modes)


# Layout Modes (/docs/guide/layout-modes)





Overview [#overview]

DiaX ships two synchronous component layouts plus an experimental asynchronous ELK `LayoutPlan`
adapter. Pick the built-in mode that matches ordinary application data; choose ELK when preserving
its stronger pixel placement, ports, route sections, and labels justifies async layout.

| Layout      | Component                      | Best for                                                 | Algorithm                       |
| ----------- | ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| **Flow**    | `<FlowDiagram>`                | Ordinary DAG pipelines, architectures, state transitions | Layered grid + planned routes   |
| **Mindmap** | `<Mindmap>`                    | Topic maps, brainstorms, hierarchies                     | Center-outward radial           |
| **ELK**     | `computeLayoutPlan` + renderer | Dense transitions, strict ports, exact edge sections     | ELK.js, opt-in and asynchronous |

Chronological participant/message sequences are not a third Core layout mode. In React, author the
participant columns and message rows as semantic DOM, then use
[Connect](/docs/react/connect#sequence-style-protocols-without-a-sequence-mode) for the measured
message rails and a narrow-screen transcript.

***

Flow Layout [#flow-layout]

The default. Computes a directed acyclic graph (DAG), stabilizes layer order, places disconnected
components in separate bands, and plans long, parallel, feedback, and labeled routes around measured
DOM nodes. Supports all four directions: `horizontal`, `vertical`, `horizontal-reverse`, and
`vertical-reverse`.

<DiagramPreview
  name="ci-pipeline"
  title="CI/CD Pipeline — Flow Layout"
  code="`<FlowDiagram
nodes={[
  { id: 'src', content: 'Code Push' },
  { id: 'lint', content: 'Lint' },
  { id: 'test', content: 'Test' },
  { id: 'build', content: 'Build' },
  { id: 'deploy', content: 'Deploy' },
]}
relations={[
  'src->lint', 'src->test',
  'lint->build', 'test->build',
  'build->deploy',
]}
centered stagger density=&#x22;spacious&#x22;
/>`"
>
  <FlowDiagram
    nodes="[
    { id: 'src', content: 'Code Push' },
    { id: 'lint', content: 'Lint' },
    { id: 'test', content: 'Test' },
    { id: 'build', content: 'Build' },
    { id: 'deploy', content: 'Deploy' },
  ]"
    relations="[
    'src->lint',
    'src->test',
    'lint->build',
    'test->build',
    'build->deploy',
  ]"
    density="spacious"
  />
</DiagramPreview>

**When to use Flow:**

* Pipelines, CI/CD, data processing
* Service architectures (API → Auth → DB)
* Any directed flow from source to sink

***

Mindmap Layout [#mindmap-layout]

Places the root node at the center and branches outward radially. The node with the highest degree automatically becomes the root.

<DiagramPreview
  name="mindmap"
  title="Platform Mindmap — Radial Layout"
  code="`<Mindmap
nodes={[
  { id: 'core', content: 'Platform' },
  { id: 'fe', content: 'Frontend' },
  { id: 'be', content: 'Backend' },
  { id: 'infra', content: 'Infrastructure' },
  { id: 'react', content: 'React' },
  { id: 'vue', content: 'Vue' },
  { id: 'api', content: 'API' },
  { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
]}
relations={[
  'core->fe', 'core->be', 'core->infra',
  'fe->react', 'fe->vue',
  'be->api', 'be->db',
]}
density=&#x22;comfortable&#x22;
/>`"
>
  <Mindmap
    nodes="[
    { id: 'core', content: 'Platform' },
    { id: 'fe', content: 'Frontend' },
    { id: 'be', content: 'Backend' },
    { id: 'infra', content: 'Infrastructure' },
    { id: 'react', content: 'React' },
    { id: 'vue', content: 'Vue' },
    { id: 'api', content: 'API' },
    { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
  ]"
    relations="[
    'core->fe',
    'core->be',
    'core->infra',
    'fe->react',
    'fe->vue',
    'be->api',
    'be->db',
  ]"
    density="comfortable"
  />
</DiagramPreview>

**When to use Mindmap:**

* Topic exploration and brainstorming
* Technology stacks and ecosystems
* Organizational hierarchies (centered)
* Any tree-like structure radiating from a hub

***

ELK Layout (Advanced) [#elk-layout-advanced]

For graphs that need stronger ordering and routing, `@diax/layout-elk` asynchronously returns the
same engine-neutral `LayoutPlan` used by DiaX's measured renderer seam. It is not a `layout` string
on `FlowDiagram`, so ELK is never loaded accidentally.

<Callout type="warn">
  Experimental: React `DiagramEdges` can consume a complete external plan today. Other adapters
  measure labels and retain prior routes for the built-in planner, but do not yet expose external
  plan rendering.
</Callout>

<InstallTabs packages="['@diax/layout-elk']" description="Experimental ELK.js LayoutPlan adapter" />

```tsx
import { elkLayout } from '@diax/layout-elk';
import { parseRelations, type DiaxNode, type NodeRect } from 'diax';

const nodes: DiaxNode<string>[] = [
  { id: 'gateway', content: 'API Gateway' },
  { id: 'service', content: 'Orders Service' },
];
const relations = [
  { id: 'gateway-service', from: 'gateway', to: 'service', label: 'HTTPS' },
];
const edges = parseRelations(relations);
const nodeSizes = new Map<string, Pick<NodeRect, 'width' | 'height'>>([
  ['gateway', { width: 160, height: 56 }],
  ['service', { width: 160, height: 56 }],
]);
const labelSizes = new Map([
  ['gateway-service', { width: 64, height: 24 }],
]);

const plan = await elkLayout({ algorithm: 'layered', direction: 'horizontal' })
  .computeLayoutPlan(nodes, edges, { nodeSizes, labelSizes });
```

**When to use ELK:**

* Highly congested rank transitions and complex fan-in/fan-out
* Strict or numerous ports whose ordering affects crossings
* Preserving orthogonal edge sections and label coordinates
* Accepting an asynchronous, opt-in layout boundary

<Callout type="warn">
  Compound groups now reserve exclusive row bands in the built-in flow layout, while ELK preserves
  native compound bounds in `LayoutPlan.groups`. Both plans derive ordered group entry/exit ports;
  collapse behavior, authored portals, and nested Connect surfaces remain outside the current
  interface.
</Callout>

See the [ELK Layout guide](/docs/guide/layout-elk) for full API details.

***

Decision Guide [#decision-guide]

Not sure which to pick? Here's a quick decision tree:

<DiagramPreview
  title="Which layout should I use?"
  code="`<FlowDiagram
nodes={[
  { id: 'start', content: 'What shape is your data?' },
  { id: 'directed', content: 'Directed flow? (A→B→C)' },
  { id: 'radial', content: 'Hub with branches?' },
  { id: 'complex', content: 'Dense transitions or strict ports?' },
  { id: 'flow', content: '✅ FlowDiagram' },
  { id: 'mindmap', content: '✅ Mindmap' },
  { id: 'elk', content: '✅ ELK Layout' },
]}
relations={[
  'start->directed', 'start->radial', 'start->complex',
  'directed->flow', 'radial->mindmap', 'complex->elk',
]}
centered density=&#x22;spacious&#x22;
/>`"
>
  <FlowDiagram
    nodes="[
    { id: 'start', content: 'What shape is your data?' },
    { id: 'directed', content: 'Directed flow? (A→B→C)' },
    { id: 'radial', content: 'Hub with branches?' },
    { id: 'complex', content: 'Dense transitions or strict ports?' },
    { id: 'flow', content: '✅ FlowDiagram' },
    { id: 'mindmap', content: '✅ Mindmap' },
    { id: 'elk', content: '✅ ELK Layout' },
  ]"
    relations="[
    'start->directed',
    'start->radial',
    'start->complex',
    'directed->flow',
    'radial->mindmap',
    'complex->elk',
  ]"
    density="spacious"
  />
</DiagramPreview>

***

Framework Support [#framework-support]

Flow and Mindmap are integrated across every supported framework. ELK is always an explicit
asynchronous pre-computation step, not a third component layout mode. React can render the complete
plan directly; other adapters currently use the compatibility bridge or a custom renderer.

| Layout  |                    React                    |                       Vue                      |                         Svelte                        |                      Solid                     |                 Vanilla                |
| ------- | :-----------------------------------------: | :--------------------------------------------: | :---------------------------------------------------: | :--------------------------------------------: | :------------------------------------: |
| Flow    |               `<FlowDiagram>`               |         `<FlowDiagram>` / `useDiagram`         |         `<FlowDiagram>` / `createFlowDiagram`         |         `<FlowDiagram>` / `useDiagram`         |             `createDiagram`            |
| Mindmap |                 `<Mindmap>`                 | `<Mindmap>` / `useDiagram({layout:'mindmap'})` | `<Mindmap>` / `createFlowDiagram({layout:'mindmap'})` | `<Mindmap>` / `useDiagram({layout:'mindmap'})` |   `createDiagram({layout:'mindmap'})`  |
| ELK     | Complete plan via `DiagramEdges layoutPlan` |     Compatibility bridge / custom renderer     |         Compatibility bridge / custom renderer        |     Compatibility bridge / custom renderer     | Compatibility bridge / custom renderer |

***

  <Card title="Edge Types" href="/docs/guide/edge-types" description="Animation presets, path types, and labels" />

  <Card title="ELK Layout" href="/docs/guide/layout-elk" description="Advanced layout with ELK.js" />
