# MDX Integration (/docs/guide/mdx-guide)



Choose the authoring path [#choose-the-authoring-path]

MDX already supports JSX, so most React documentation sites do not need a DiaX-specific MDX
package. Choose by the source you already own:

| Source                                                        | Recommended path                  | Why                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Nodes and relations from frontmatter, an API or reviewed data | `@diax/react`                     | Keep one serializable topology and render rich DOM content               |
| A small topology authored directly beside the prose           | `@diax/react/jsx`                 | Concise JSX syntax for a static visual explanation                       |
| Existing Mermaid fences in trusted source files               | `remark-diax`                     | Transform supported fences during the MDX build and report invalid input |
| Untrusted AI or user output                                   | Validated JSON into `@diax/react` | Do not execute generated MDX, imports or JSX                             |

<Callout type="warn">
  MDX is application source: it can execute JavaScript and JSX. Compile AI-generated MDX only
  after review. For untrusted runtime output, accept a constrained JSON schema, validate it, and map
  known values to application-owned components.
</Callout>

Plain MDX composition [#plain-mdx-composition]

Install the React binding and import it in the MDX file or register it in the site's shared MDX
component map.

<InstallTabs packages="['@diax/react']" description="React binding for data-first diagrams in trusted MDX" />

This complete component is checked by the documentation contract:

```tsx title="components/RequestPathDiagram.tsx" contract
import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

export function RequestPathDiagram() {
  return (
    <FlowDiagram
      nodes={[
        { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
        { id: 'api', content: 'API' },
        { id: 'database', content: 'Database' },
      ]}
      relations={['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|database']}
      density="comfortable"
    />
  );
}
```

Then import the component from a trusted `.mdx` document:

```mdx title="content/architecture.mdx"
import { RequestPathDiagram } from '../components/RequestPathDiagram';

# Request path

<RequestPathDiagram />
```

The MDX block is intentionally a document fragment, not a standalone TypeScript module. The
`RequestPathDiagram.tsx` module above is the copy-pasteable contract.

Register shared components [#register-shared-components]

Frameworks expose different MDX registries, but DiaX does not require a special runtime adapter.
For Fumadocs, extend its normal component map:

```tsx title="app/docs/[[...slug]]/page.tsx"
import { FlowDiagram, Mindmap } from '@diax/react';
import defaultMdxComponents from 'fumadocs-ui/mdx';

// Configuration fragment: merge this object into the page's existing MDX setup.
export const diaxMdxComponents = {
  ...defaultMdxComponents,
  FlowDiagram,
  Mindmap,
};
```

Nextra uses `mdx-components.tsx`; Docusaurus uses its MDX component scope. In all three cases, the
important contract is the same: register the public React components, keep topology in one source,
and load the component from a client boundary when the host performs server rendering.

See [React SSR](/docs/react/ssr) for Next.js and hydration requirements.

Reusable presentation [#reusable-presentation]

Extract repeated visual policy into an ordinary React component rather than repeating configuration
throughout prose:

```tsx title="components/ArchitectureDiagram.tsx" contract
import { FlowDiagram, type FlowDiagramProps } from '@diax/react';

export function ArchitectureDiagram(props: FlowDiagramProps) {
  return <FlowDiagram density="spacious" {...props} />;
}
```

Keep complex data in a `.ts` module and import it into the wrapper or MDX document. Do not map data
arrays back into `DiaxNode` and `DiaxEdge` markers; the data interface already represents that
topology directly.

Mermaid fences in trusted MDX [#mermaid-fences-in-trusted-mdx]

Use `remark-diax` when a documentation repository already owns Mermaid fences and wants automatic
build-time conversion:

<InstallTabs packages="['remark-diax', '@diax/ui-react', '@diax/react', '@diax/mermaid']" description="Build-time fence transformation plus the explicit Mermaid renderer leaf" />

Import `@diax/ui-react/styles.css` once from the host's global stylesheet. The plugin automatically
injects the `SmartMermaidDiagram` import for a valid fence; the host does not register a hidden
global component.

````md title="content/system.mdx"
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  browser[Browser] --> api[API]
  api --> database[(Database)]
```
````

Invalid or unsupported source remains visible as its original code block. The plugin also appends
standard VFile messages, allowing a live preview to show markers while CI applies a stricter policy.
It does not introduce another diagram language and it does not claim full Mermaid compatibility.

For the complete ESM setup, options, supported fence aliases, VFile fields, build policy and
Fumadocs/Docusaurus examples, use the [`remark-diax` Reference](/docs/reference/remark-diax).

Mermaid without a Remark build [#mermaid-without-a-remark-build]

For a single React MDX page, render the explicit optional leaf directly:

```tsx title="components/ImportedDiagram.tsx" contract
import { SmartMermaidDiagram } from '@diax/ui-react/mermaid';

export function ImportedDiagram() {
  return (
    <SmartMermaidDiagram
      chart={`flowchart LR
        author[Author] --> build[MDX build]
        build --> reader[Reader]`}
    />
  );
}
```

This path is often simpler than configuring a Remark plugin for one diagram. See the
[Mermaid Guide](/docs/guide/mermaid) for supported syntax and fidelity limits.

Authoring rules [#authoring-rules]

1. Keep one topology definition; use rich DOM only for presentation.
2. Put complete reusable code in `.tsx` modules and keep MDX fragments short.
3. Treat MDX as trusted executable source, never as an untrusted runtime payload.
4. Use the data interface for generated or external nodes and relations.
5. Import Mermaid and its UI renderer only on routes that need them.
6. Let VFile diagnostics drive editor markers and build policy; do not silently drop invalid fences.

Next steps [#next-steps]

* [React Guide](/docs/react) — data and JSX authoring interfaces
* [`remark-diax` Reference](/docs/reference/remark-diax) — build integration and diagnostics
* [Mermaid Import](/docs/guide/mermaid) — supported source and runtime rendering
* [AI Integration](/docs/guide/ai-integration) — validation and trust boundaries
* [Package Entry Points](/docs/reference/package-entry-points) — loading and tree-shaking boundaries


# Mermaid Import (/docs/guide/mermaid)





What DiaX supports [#what-diax-supports]

DiaX treats Mermaid as an input format, not as a renderer replacement. Mermaid defines topology;
DiaX converts the supported graph families into a typed AST and renders the nodes as real DOM.

| Mermaid family      | Header                             | DiaX preset       |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Flowchart           | `flowchart` / `graph`              | `FlowNode`        |
| Class diagram       | `classDiagram`                     | `ClassNode`       |
| State diagram       | `stateDiagram` / `stateDiagram-v2` | `StateNode`       |
| ER diagram          | `erDiagram`                        | `EntityNode`      |
| Requirement diagram | `requirementDiagram`               | `RequirementNode` |
| Mindmap             | `mindmap`                          | `MindmapNode`     |

<Callout type="warn">
  This is a supported Mermaid subset, not full Mermaid compatibility. Sequence, Gantt, Pie,
  Timeline, Sankey and other families require different domain models and layouts.
</Callout>

Render Mermaid as styled DOM [#render-mermaid-as-styled-dom]

Install the React preset and parser packages, then import the preset stylesheet once:

<InstallTabs packages="['@diax/ui-react', '@diax/react', '@diax/mermaid']" description="Styled DOM presets plus the optional Mermaid importer" />

The `@diax/ui-react` root contains only DOM presets. Mermaid compositions live at the explicit
`@diax/ui-react/mermaid` subpath, and `@diax/mermaid` is an optional peer. This keeps the parser out
of primitive-only installations and native ESM/module-federation entries. These packages are
ESM-only; CommonJS `require()` is not a declared export.

```css title="app.css"
@import '@diax/ui-react/styles.css';
```

```tsx title="architecture.tsx" contract
import { SmartMermaidDiagram } from '@diax/ui-react/mermaid';

export function Architecture() {
  return (
    <SmartMermaidDiagram
      chart={`
        flowchart LR
          browser[Browser] --> api[API]
          api --> db[(Postgres)]
      `}
    />
  );
}
```

`SmartMermaidDiagram` detects the supported family, parses it once, selects the matching preset
renderer and displays an accessible error when parsing fails.

If Mermaid is an optional mode rather than initial page content, load the leaf entry on first use.
The subpath provides a default export specifically for `React.lazy`:

```tsx title="lazy-mermaid.tsx" contract
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const SmartMermaidDiagram = lazy(() => import('@diax/ui-react/mermaid'));

export function OptionalMermaid({ chart }: { chart: string }) {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p role="status">Loading diagram…</p>}>
      <SmartMermaidDiagram chart={chart} />
    </Suspense>
  );
}
```

Declare the lazy component at module scope so its identity and cached import remain stable. Render it
only after the feature is selected; rendering it immediately creates another chunk but does not
delay its request. In Next.js, place the dynamic declaration in a Client Component when using
client-only options.

Mix Mermaid topology with application DOM [#mix-mermaid-topology-with-application-dom]

Keep topology in Mermaid and override presentation through stable Mermaid node IDs:

The following block focuses on the `renderNode` callback. `ServiceCard` and `DatabaseStatus` are
application-owned components, so this is a teaching fragment rather than a standalone module.

```tsx title="live-architecture.tsx"
import { SmartMermaidDiagram } from '@diax/ui-react/mermaid';

<SmartMermaidDiagram
  chart={`
    flowchart LR
      browser[Browser] --> api[API] --> db[(Postgres)]
  `}
  renderNode={(node, { state, defaultNode }) => {
    if (node.id === 'api') {
      return (
        <ServiceCard
          service="payments"
          healthy
          highlighted={state === 'highlighted'}
        />
      );
    }

    if (node.id === 'db') {
      return <DatabaseStatus database="orders" />;
    }

    return defaultNode;
  }}
/>
```

The contract is deliberately narrow:

* `chart` is the only topology source.
* Mermaid IDs are stable DOM override points.
* `renderNode` changes presentation, not graph structure.
* `defaultNode` preserves the built-in renderer for nodes you do not replace.
* Do not mix `chart` with JSX children that add another set of nodes or edges.

Inspect the Import Path [#inspect-the-import-path]

The runnable study keeps Mermaid as the topology source, then exposes the resulting diagram as real
DOM with inspectable source and an explicit ownership contract.

<ShowcaseStudies slugs="['mermaid-import']" />

Parse without React [#parse-without-react]

Use the high-level importer when you need the normalized AST, diagnostics or your own renderer:

```ts title="parse-mermaid.ts" contract
import { parseMermaid } from '@diax/mermaid';

const source = `flowchart LR
  browser[Browser] --> api[API]
  api --> database[(Database)]`;
const result = parseMermaid(source);

if (!result.ast) {
  for (const diagnostic of result.diagnostics) {
    console.error(
      diagnostic.code,
      diagnostic.location,
      diagnostic.message,
      diagnostic.hint,
    );
  }
  throw new Error('Invalid Mermaid input');
}

console.log(result.diagramType); // "flowchart", "classDiagram", ...
console.log(result.ast.nodes);
console.log(result.ast.edges);
console.log(result.ast.groups); // flowchart subgraphs, when present
```

The following type is a reference shape. Use the exported result types in application code rather
than copying this teaching fragment:

```ts title="result-shape.ts"
type MermaidParseResult = {
  diagramType: MermaidDiagramType | null;
  ast: DiaxAST<string> | null;
  diagnostics: MermaidDiagnostic[];
};
```

The importer does not guess a different parser when it sees an unsupported header. For example,
`sequenceDiagram` produces an `UNSUPPORTED_DIAGRAM_TYPE` diagnostic with the header location and
a caller-actionable repair hint. Mermaid diagnostics use the same `severity`, `message`, `location`
and `hint` contract as Core diagnostics.

This is specifically an importer boundary, not a claim that DiaX cannot express chronological
protocols. React users can author semantic participant columns and message rows with the
[Connect sequence recipe](/docs/react/connect#sequence-style-protocols-without-a-sequence-mode).

Flowchart-only compatibility interface [#flowchart-only-compatibility-interface]

Existing applications that rely on the old `{ nodes, relations }` flowchart result can migrate
without ambiguity:

```ts contract
import {
  parseMermaidFlowchart,
  parseMermaidFlowchartBlock,
} from '@diax/mermaid';

const { nodes, relations } = parseMermaidFlowchart(`
  flowchart LR
    A[Start] --> B[Finish]
`);
```

The explicit name prevents a flowchart-only parser from being mistaken for the multi-family
importer. New code should prefer `parseMermaid()` or `SmartMermaidDiagram`.

Error handling [#error-handling]

The React entry provides a visible default error, an observability callback and a custom fallback:

This callback-only fragment assumes application-owned `generatedSource`, `reportDiagramError`, and
`DiagramError` bindings:

```tsx
import type { MermaidDiagnostic } from '@diax/mermaid';

<SmartMermaidDiagram
  chart={generatedSource}
  onError={(error) => reportDiagramError(error)}
  fallback={(error) => {
    const diagnostic = error.cause as MermaidDiagnostic | undefined;
    return (
      <DiagramError
        title="Diagram could not be rendered"
        hint={diagnostic?.hint}
      >
        {error.message}
      </DiagramError>
    );
  }}
/>
```

This matters for AI-generated diagrams: invalid output must be diagnosable and testable rather than
turning into an unexplained blank region. `error.cause` contains the original
`MermaidDiagnostic`, including its stable code, source location and repair hint.

Current fidelity limits [#current-fidelity-limits]

The importer preserves basic topology, labels, direction, supported edge markers and flowchart
subgraph containment, but some Mermaid semantics remain intentionally limited:

* Subgraphs render as derived rectangular boundaries in the React composition. Compound routing,
  collapsed groups and group ports are not yet preserved.
* `style`, `classDef`, `click` and `linkStyle` are not equivalent to application DOM behavior.
* Composite states and other advanced state semantics are not fully modeled.
* Class, ER, requirement and mindmap structured metadata are still being deepened for lossless DOM
  presets.
* Final SVG edge paths require client-side DOM measurement, even when topology and Grid placement
  are server-rendered.

Use the compatibility limits above when deciding whether to import Mermaid or author DiaX topology
directly. Unsupported Mermaid families should remain on Mermaid or use a domain-specific renderer.

<Cards>
  <Card title="UI presets" href="/docs/ui-react" description="Styled DOM nodes for six supported graph families" />

  <Card title="SmartMermaidDiagram" href="/docs/ui-react/smart-mermaid" description="Live examples, node overrides and error behavior" />

  <Card title="MDX integration" href="/docs/guide/mdx-guide" description="Turn fenced Mermaid blocks into DiaX components" />
</Cards>


# Migration Guide (/docs/guide/migration)



Pre-1.0 Theme Import Migration [#pre-10-theme-import-migration]

Theme authoring moved out of the headless `diax` root and into `diax/themes`. Framework users who
only pass `theme="github"` do not need to change component code.

```diff
- import { lightTheme, themeToCSS } from 'diax';
+ import { themes, themeToCSS } from 'diax/themes';

- const css = themeToCSS(lightTheme);
+ const css = themeToCSS(themes.light);
```

The global `registerTheme()`, `getTheme()` and `getThemeNames()` functions were removed. Pass custom
themes as values so SSR, multiple bundles and Module Federation remotes cannot observe divergent
registries:

```tsx
import type { DiaxTheme } from 'diax/themes';

const brand: DiaxTheme = {
  name: 'brand',
  light: { '--diax-node-bg': '#fff', '--diax-node-text': '#111827' },
  dark: { '--diax-node-bg': '#111827', '--diax-node-text': '#f9fafb' },
};

<FlowDiagram theme={brand} nodes={nodes} relations={relations} />;
```

Pre-1.0 Framework Interface Migration [#pre-10-framework-interface-migration]

The React root no longer exports its internal generic `Diagram`, the shallow `useDiagramBuilder`
state wrapper, or the `useTheme` convenience hook:

```diff
- import { Diagram, useDiagramBuilder, useTheme } from '@diax/react';
+ import { FlowDiagram, type ThemeInput } from '@diax/react';
```

Use `FlowDiagram` or `Mindmap` for the high-level rendering lifecycle. Keep dynamic nodes and
relations in ordinary `useState`/`useReducer` or an application store, and keep theme selection in
ordinary React state. The low-level `useDiagram` + `DiagramCanvas` + `DiagramNode` + `DiagramEdges`
composition remains public for custom renderers.

React JSX topology moved to its own authoring entry. The syntax remains supported and now exposes
the complete shared Relation contract; only the import changes:

```diff
- import { DiaxEdge, DiaxNode, FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';
+ import { DiaxEdge, DiaxNode, FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react/jsx';
```

The root `@diax/react` `FlowDiagram` now accepts data only. If nodes and relations already exist as
arrays, keep the root import and pass them directly instead of mapping them into JSX markers.

Rich edge events now live only on relation objects. If you used the low-level React
`DiagramEdges.edgeEvents` map, move each handler onto the corresponding relation. This also gives
parallel edges an unambiguous event owner and enables the same behavior in all official adapters:

```diff
- const edgeEvents = new Map([
-   ['client→api', { onClick: handleOpen }],
- ]);
- <DiagramEdges edges={edges} layoutMap={layoutMap} edgeEvents={edgeEvents} />
+ const edges = [{ from: 'client', to: 'api', onClick: handleOpen }];
+ <DiagramEdges edges={edges} layoutMap={layoutMap} />
```

Vue and Solid no longer export `useTheme`. Theme selection is ordinary framework state; replace the
wrapper with Vue `ref<ThemeInput>()` or Solid `createSignal<ThemeInput>()`, then pass the value to
`FlowDiagram`. This keeps Theme policy out of framework roots and avoids a second state abstraction.

Vue's low-level `useEdgeRenderer()` now returns Core render data without a translation layer. Update
custom SVG renderers to the resolved names below:

| Before                          | Now                                     |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `path.color`                    | `path.displayColor`                     |
| `path.markerEnd`                | `path.markerEndUrl`                     |
| `path.markerStart`              | `path.markerStartUrl`                   |
| `marker.viewBox`                | `marker.def.viewBox`                    |
| `marker.refX` / `marker.refY`   | `marker.def.refX` / `marker.def.refY`   |
| `marker.path` / `marker.filled` | `marker.def.path` / `marker.def.filled` |

The composable no longer accepts or returns a global `strokeWidth`; set the visible path width from
`path.strokeWidth` with your renderer's own fallback. It now returns only `{ paths, markers }`.

Solid custom renderers now receive Accessors. This follows Solid's fine-grained reactivity model and
keeps authored node DOM, focus and local state stable when highlight state changes:

```diff
  renderNode={(node, state) => (
-   <Card dimmed={state === 'dimmed'}>{node.content}</Card>
+   <Card dimmed={state() === 'dimmed'}>{node().content}</Card>
  )}
```

Apply the same `node()` / `state()` change to functions in a Solid `nodeTypes` registry.

The Core `getNodeDisplayOpacity()` helper now returns `0.25` for a dimmed node (previously `0.2`).
All official adapters consume that single policy, matching the existing `opacity-25` renderer
examples and preventing framework-specific visual drift.

Pre-1.0 Mermaid Importer Migration [#pre-10-mermaid-importer-migration]

The concrete `mermaidAstAdapter` and its parser-adapter type are now internal. Normal callers should
use the deep importer; a tool that already knows the diagram family can use the corresponding
transformer directly:

```diff
- import { mermaidAstAdapter } from '@diax/mermaid';
- const type = mermaidAstAdapter.detect(source);
- const ast = type === 'flowchart'
-   ? mermaidAstAdapter.parseFlowchart(source)
-   : null;
+ import { parseMermaid } from '@diax/mermaid';
+ const { diagramType: type, ast, diagnostics } = parseMermaid(source);
```

```diff
- import { mermaidAstAdapter } from '@diax/mermaid';
- const ast = mermaidAstAdapter.parseClassDiagram(source);
+ import { transformClassDiagram } from '@diax/mermaid';
+ const ast = transformClassDiagram(source);
```

Parser backend replacement is not a public plugin lifecycle. `parseMermaid()` owns detection,
dispatch, empty-input handling and diagnostics so tools do not reproduce that coordination.

Migrating from Mermaid [#migrating-from-mermaid]

DiaX can import a supported Mermaid subset into a normalized `DiaxAST`. The importer currently covers
flowchart, class, state, ER, requirement and mindmap families; it is not a full Mermaid renderer.

Before (Mermaid) [#before-mermaid]

```html
<pre class="mermaid">
graph LR
  A[Browser] -->|HTTPS| B[API Server]
  B -->|SQL| C[Database]
  B -->|gRPC| D[Auth Service]
</pre>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid/dist/mermaid.min.js"></script>
```

After (DiaX) [#after-diax]

If you previously imported the high-level component from `@diax/ui-react`, move that import to
`@diax/ui-react/mermaid`. The root now intentionally contains only parser-free DOM presets.

Install `@diax/ui-react`, `@diax/react` and `@diax/mermaid`, import
`@diax/ui-react/styles.css` once from the application's global stylesheet, and render the existing
source through the supported-subset component:

```tsx
import { SmartMermaidDiagram } from '@diax/ui-react/mermaid';

const chart = `
  graph LR
    A[Browser] -->|HTTPS| B[API Server]
    B -->|SQL| C[Database]
    B -->|gRPC| D[Auth Service]
`;

function MyDiagram() {
  return <SmartMermaidDiagram chart={chart} />;
}
```

Use `parseMermaid()` when a migration tool, CI check or custom renderer needs the normalized AST and
diagnostics rather than a React component:

```ts
import { parseMermaid } from '@diax/mermaid';

const result = parseMermaid(chart);

if (!result.ast) {
  throw new Error(JSON.stringify(result.diagnostics));
}

console.log(result.diagramType, result.ast.nodes, result.ast.edges);
```

The AST contains `nodes`, normalized `edges` and optional layout metadata. It does not return the
legacy `{ nodes, relations }` shape; that shape belongs only to the explicitly named
`parseMermaidFlowchart()` compatibility function.

Or skip Mermaid import and write the topology directly in DiaX:

```tsx
import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

function MyDiagram() {
  return (
    <FlowDiagram
      nodes={[
        { id: 'browser', content: 'Browser' },
        { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
        { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
        { id: 'auth', content: 'Auth Service' },
      ]}
      relations={['browser->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db', 'api->|gRPC|auth']}
    />
  );
}
```

Key Differences [#key-differences]

| Mermaid                   | DiaX                                              |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| String DSL only           | JSON, JSX, or string DSL                          |
| SVG output (opaque)       | Real DOM nodes (styleable)                        |
| `graph LR` / `graph TD`   | `direction="horizontal"` / `direction="vertical"` |
| `-->` (dashed in Mermaid) | `-->` (dashed in DiaX too)                        |
| `-->\|label\|`            | `->\|label\|` or `{ label: '...' }`               |
| Theme via CSS variables   | Theme presets + full CSS control                  |

***

Migrating from react-archer [#migrating-from-react-archer]

First decide who should own placement. If your flex, grid, Tailwind and semantic HTML are part of the
visual explanation, migrate to Connect and keep that DOM. If the CSS only arranged generic boxes and
you want the library to place them, migrate to automatic Diagram instead.

react-archer puts outgoing relations on source wrappers. Connect keeps endpoints on the real DOM but
moves topology into one reviewable relation list.

Before (react-archer) [#before-react-archer]

```tsx
import { ArcherContainer, ArcherElement } from 'react-archer';

function MyDiagram() {
  return (
    <ArcherContainer strokeColor="#999">
      <div style={{ display: 'flex', gap: 80 }}>
        <ArcherElement
          id="client"
          relations={[
            { targetId: 'api', targetAnchor: 'left', sourceAnchor: 'right' },
          ]}
        >
          <div className="box">Client</div>
        </ArcherElement>
        <ArcherElement
          id="api"
          relations={[
            { targetId: 'db', targetAnchor: 'left', sourceAnchor: 'right' },
          ]}
        >
          <div className="box">API</div>
        </ArcherElement>
        <ArcherElement id="db">
          <div className="box">Database</div>
        </ArcherElement>
      </div>
    </ArcherContainer>
  );
}
```

After: keep the authored layout with Connect [#after-keep-the-authored-layout-with-connect]

```tsx title="archer-migration.tsx" contract
'use client';

import type { DiaxRelation } from 'diax';
import { ConnectionSurface, connectionTarget } from '@diax/react/connect';

const relations = [
  { from: 'client', to: 'api', targetMarker: 'arrow' },
  { from: 'api', to: 'db', targetMarker: 'arrow' },
] satisfies readonly DiaxRelation[];

function MyDiagram() {
  return (
    <ConnectionSurface relations={relations} className="grid grid-cols-3 gap-20">
      <section {...connectionTarget('client')} className="box">Client</section>
      <section {...connectionTarget('api')} className="box">API</section>
      <section {...connectionTarget('db')} className="box">Database</section>
    </ConnectionSurface>
  );
}
```

Start without anchor overrides. Connect chooses facing edges from the measured boxes and keeps them
updated as the authored layout reflows. Add an explicit anchor only when one attachment side carries
real meaning, not as routine migration boilerplate.

Alternative: hand placement to Diagram [#alternative-hand-placement-to-diagram]

When the old flex/grid was incidental, use `FlowDiagram` with the same centralized relations:

```tsx
import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

<FlowDiagram
  nodes={[
    { id: 'client', content: 'Client' },
    { id: 'api', content: 'API' },
    { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
  ]}
  relations={['client->api', 'api->db']}
/>;
```

Key Differences [#key-differences-1]

| react-archer                      | DiaX Connect                                            | DiaX Diagram                                  |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Application owns flex/grid        | Application still owns flex/grid                        | DiaX owns placement                           |
| Relations live on source wrappers | Relations are centralized                               | Relations are centralized                     |
| Every endpoint needs a wrapper    | Attribute lands on the real DOM element                 | Nodes are definition data                     |
| Anchors are commonly repeated     | Facing anchors are automatic; overrides remain optional | Layout and anchors are automatic              |
| React only                        | React-only authored-DOM leaf                            | Framework-agnostic Core + five Alpha adapters |

***

Migrating from D2 [#migrating-from-d2]

D2 is a CLI tool, so migration is about translating concepts rather than replacing imports.

Concept Mapping [#concept-mapping]

| D2                     | DiaX                                          |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `.d2` file             | JSX component or JSON                         |
| `a -> b: label`        | `'a->\|label\|b'`                             |
| `a -- b`               | `{ from: 'a', to: 'b', bidirectional: true }` |
| `a.style.fill: "#red"` | `renderNode` or `nodeTypes`                   |
| `d2 compile input.d2`  | Import and render in your app                 |
| `direction: right`     | `direction="horizontal"`                      |
| `direction: down`      | `direction="vertical"`                        |

Before (D2) [#before-d2]

```text
direction: right

client: Browser
api: API Server
db: PostgreSQL
auth: Auth Service

client -> api: HTTPS
api -> db: SQL
api -> auth: gRPC
```

After (DiaX) [#after-diax-1]

```tsx
import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

function MyDiagram() {
  return (
    <FlowDiagram
      direction="horizontal"
      nodes={[
        { id: 'client', content: 'Browser' },
        { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
        { id: 'db', content: 'PostgreSQL' },
        { id: 'auth', content: 'Auth Service' },
      ]}
      relations={['client->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db', 'api->|gRPC|auth']}
    />
  );
}
```

The main advantage of migrating: your diagrams become **live components** in your web app instead of static image assets.


# Performance (/docs/guide/performance)



Re-render Strategies [#re-render-strategies]

DiaX computes topology layout and routing in JavaScript. DOM measurement and final SVG rendering
remain on the main thread. The current packages do not silently create a Web Worker.

Because DiaX utilizes standard CSS Grid for positioning nodes rather than `absolute/transform` values, browser layout recalculation is extremely batched and highly performant.

Node Count Guidelines [#node-count-guidelines]

| Node Count | Performance        | Recommendation                                                                      |
| ---------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1–50       | Instant            | Default settings, no optimization needed                                            |
| 50–200     | Fast               | Consider `measureMode="resize"` (default)                                           |
| 200–500    | Good               | Use `measureMode="resize"`, avoid `highlightOnHover` for all nodes                  |
| 500+       | Measure long tasks | Consider the explicit ELK adapter; worker execution is not yet a built-in interface |

The built-in planner uses linear rank assignment followed by a fixed number of stable
crossing-minimization sweeps. Layer ordering uses an inversion count instead of comparing every
edge pair. Obstacle-aware gate selection only scores routes from the same rank transition, and only
while that transition contains at most 16 already-planned routes. Denser transitions keep a
deterministic obstacle-aware gate without unbounded pairwise scoring.

This is a bounded visual heuristic, not a promise that every planner stage has one universal
complexity or millisecond figure. Measure representative graphs in your own browser and device
class. If a few rank transitions are exceptionally dense, or the graph needs compound boundaries
and strict port ordering, use the explicit ELK adapter.

Worker evaluation [#worker-evaluation]

`pnpm perf:layout:worker` compares main-thread execution with a warm Node worker and separately
measures definition, measured-geometry, `LayoutPlan` clone, and final render costs. Representative
local Node 22 runs on 2026-07-24, after bounded obstacle-gate routing was enabled, found:

| Fixture                   |      Main total | Warm worker round trip | Final render after worker | Plan returned to main |
| ------------------------- | --------------: | ---------------------: | ------------------------: | --------------------: |
| 500 nodes / 1,000 edges   |   about 70–71ms |          about 63–68ms |               about 3–4ms |                 656KB |
| 1,000 nodes / 2,000 edges | about 135–139ms |        about 133–142ms |                 about 4ms |                1.30MB |

The warm-worker round trip excludes the final main-thread SVG geometry render shown in the next
column. At 500 nodes it can move the layout long task off the main thread while ending at roughly
the same total latency; at 1,000 nodes the measured end-to-end path is slower. It also adds
clone/memory cost. DiaX therefore does not expose `worker: true` today. A future worker adapter must
be a separately loaded leaf, reuse a warm worker, discard stale versioned results, and prove browser
long-task improvement. Its messages must contain only serializable IDs, endpoints and measured
numbers—not React nodes or event callbacks. Connect must remain independent from it.

The Measure Mode Cost [#the-measure-mode-cost]

During initialization or node resizing, DiaX relies on DOM dimension measurements to place SVG edges exactly at the node boundary.

If using the default config, `measureMode` is `"resize"` (backed by a native `ResizeObserver`).

```tsx
<FlowDiagram measureMode="resize" /> // [!code highlight]
```

If your node styles load lazily (e.g. late fonts, images without strict dimensions), the node size will pop, making edges appear misaligned initially.
You can bump the engine to `"auto"` which binds `MutationObserver` alongside `animationend` hooks for highly dynamic internal content.

Using `"continuous"` binds a `requestAnimationFrame` polling loop. It can keep endpoints attached
during active motion, but it does not improve graph ordering or edge routing and it consumes CPU
for as long as it is enabled. &#x2A;*Only use continuous while a node is actively being dragged, then
return to `"resize"` or `"auto"`.**

MeasureMode Decision Guide [#measuremode-decision-guide]

| Mode           | Observer                              | CPU     | Best For                             |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `"resize"`     | ResizeObserver                        | Lowest  | Static diagrams, SSR pages           |
| `"auto"`       | + MutationObserver + animation events | Medium  | Stagger animations, dynamic content  |
| `"continuous"` | + requestAnimationFrame loop          | Highest | Drag interactions, real-time updates |

Stagger Animation Performance [#stagger-animation-performance]

When `stagger` is enabled, DiaX auto-upgrades `measureMode` to `"auto"` to capture animation-end events. The stagger overhead is proportional to the number of columns (not nodes):

* Each column triggers one `setTimeout` + one re-measure
* For a 10-column diagram with 100ms stagger delay: \~1s total animation time

SSR Initialization [#ssr-initialization]

If rendering on the server, the backend doesn't possess HTML DOM metrics. Diagram calculations are strictly bypassed until the first `useEffect / onMount`.

To avoid layout shift, define strict `min-height / min-width` on your nodes using CSS so that the layout pre-computes without waiting for asynchronous font loading.

Bundle Size Optimization [#bundle-size-optimization]

The core `diax` package is tree-shakeable. If you only need layout computation without edge rendering:

```ts
// Imports the Core Diagram computation interface without React or Mermaid.
import { computeLayout } from 'diax';
```

For the full breakdown of package sizes, see the [Packages section](/) on the homepage.


# Philosophy (/docs/guide/philosophy)





The Product Gap [#the-product-gap]

Existing tools optimize for different jobs:

* **Mermaid** prioritizes a portable text DSL and a consistent SVG renderer.
* **D2** prioritizes declarative source and compiled SVG/PNG output.
* **React Flow** provides a capable interactive editor surface with positioned React nodes.
* **Excalidraw** prioritizes free-form visual sketching.

The remaining gap is code-defined diagrams whose nodes must be ordinary application DOM: existing
design-system components, semantic HTML, live state and responsive CSS should remain usable without
giving the diagram runtime ownership of their presentation.

The Insight [#the-insight]

> **Structure and presentation should be completely decoupled.**

This is the same insight that powers:

* **Headless UI** (Radix) — behavior without styling
* **Headless CMS** (Sanity) — content without rendering
* **CSS-in-JS** — styling as data, not files

DiaX applies this to diagrams:

* **You describe** the structure (nodes, edges, relations)
* **DiaX computes** the layout (positions, paths, coordinates)
* **You render** with your own JSX, Tailwind, Vue templates, or vanilla DOM

There are two ownership modes behind that idea:

* **Diagram mode** — you provide topology and node content; DiaX also owns automatic layout.
* **Connect mode** — you keep an existing DOM/CSS layout; DiaX only measures and connects targets.

Both are public, but they remain separate loading seams: Diagram components come from `@diax/react`;
authored-DOM connection comes from `@diax/react/connect`. Neither interface silently switches layout
ownership based on props or child shape.

<DiagramPreview
  title="Separation of Concerns"
  code="`<FlowDiagram
nodes={[
  { id: 'describe', content: 'You Describe' },
  { id: 'compute', content: 'DiaX Computes' },
  { id: 'render', content: 'You Render' },
]}
relations={[
  'describe->|nodes, edges|compute',
  'compute->|positions, paths|render',
]}
centered density=&#x22;spacious&#x22;
style={{ gap: '16px 80px' }}
/>`"
>
  <FlowDiagram
    nodes="[
    { id: 'describe', content: 'You Describe' },
    { id: 'compute', content: 'DiaX Computes' },
    { id: 'render', content: 'You Render' },
  ]"
    relations="[
    'describe->|nodes, edges|compute',
    'compute->|positions, paths|render',
  ]"
    density="spacious"
    style="{ gap: '16px 80px' }"
  />
</DiagramPreview>

MDX + JSX + Tailwind + DiaX [#mdx--jsx--tailwind--diax]

This combination is a strong fit for trusted, code-reviewed technical content:

```mdx title="my-page.mdx"
import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

# System Architecture

Here's how our services connect:

<FlowDiagram
  nodes={[
    { id: 'api', content: 'API Gateway' },
    { id: 'auth', content: 'Auth Service' },
    { id: 'db', content: 'PostgreSQL' },
  ]}
  relations={['api->auth', 'auth->|JWT|db']}
  density="spacious"
/>
```

Why this works:

1. **Markdown for prose** — headings, paragraphs, lists, links
2. **JSX for diagrams** — interactive, type-safe, component-based
3. **Tailwind for styling** — consistent design system, utility classes
4. **DiaX for layout** — automatic positioning, edge routing, animations

The result: diagrams that look like they belong in your product, not like they were generated by a separate tool.

MDX and JSX are executable application source. They belong in a trusted authoring and review
workflow; untrusted model output should cross the application boundary as validated JSON instead.

AI-Native Design [#ai-native-design]

DiaX is designed from the ground up for the AI era:

```json title="AI-friendly JSON"
{
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "browser", "content": "Browser" },
    { "id": "api", "content": "API Server" }
  ],
  "relations": [
    { "from": "browser", "to": "api", "label": "HTTPS" }
  ]
}
```

This JSON is:

* **Easy for LLMs to generate** — simple nodes and explicit object edges
* **Easy to validate** — a runtime schema checks structure and DiaX diagnostics check graph semantics
* **Easy to render** — pass only validated `nodes` and `relations` to `FlowDiagram`

TypeScript types do not validate JSON at runtime. Parse model output as `unknown`, enforce size and
field allowlists, then render it as data. See the [AI Integration guide](/docs/guide/ai-integration)
for the full trust-boundary workflow.

Design Principles [#design-principles]

<DiagramPreview
  title="DiaX Design Principles"
  code="`<Mindmap
nodes={[
  { id: 'core', content: 'DiaX Principles' },
  { id: 'headless', content: 'Headless' },
  { id: 'progressive', content: 'Progressive' },
  { id: 'agnostic', content: 'Agnostic' },
  { id: 'tiny', content: 'Tiny' },
  { id: 'accessible', content: 'Accessible' },
  { id: 'compat', content: 'Compatible' },
]}
relations={[
  'core->headless', 'core->progressive',
  'core->agnostic', 'core->tiny',
  'core->accessible', 'core->compat',
]}
density=&#x22;comfortable&#x22;
/>`"
>
  <Mindmap
    nodes="[
    { id: 'core', content: 'DiaX Principles' },
    { id: 'headless', content: 'Headless' },
    { id: 'progressive', content: 'Progressive' },
    { id: 'agnostic', content: 'Agnostic' },
    { id: 'tiny', content: 'Tiny' },
    { id: 'accessible', content: 'Accessible' },
    { id: 'compat', content: 'Compatible' },
  ]"
    relations="[
    'core->headless',
    'core->progressive',
    'core->agnostic',
    'core->tiny',
    'core->accessible',
    'core->compat',
  ]"
    density="comfortable"
  />
</DiagramPreview>

1\. Headless Core, DOM Bindings [#1-headless-core-dom-bindings]

The `diax` core computes topology, bindings and edge geometry. Framework packages turn those results
into real DOM nodes plus an SVG connection layer, while the application remains responsible for node
content and styling.

2\. Progressive Disclosure [#2-progressive-disclosure]

* **Quick Start**: `<FlowDiagram>` / `<Mindmap>` — current Alpha compatibility entry points
* **Custom Rendering**: `renderNode` — custom styling, same layout
* **Headless**: `useDiagram()` — binding data for library authors and advanced rendering

Start simple, go deep when you need to.

3\. Framework Agnostic Core [#3-framework-agnostic-core]

The `diax` core package is pure TypeScript with zero runtime dependencies. The adapters are not yet
interchangeable in every capability:

| Package         | Current role            | Reactive primitive |
| --------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------ |
| `@diax/react`   | Reference Alpha binding | hooks              |
| `@diax/vue`     | Official Alpha adapter  | computed/ref       |
| `@diax/svelte`  | Official Alpha adapter  | stores             |
| `@diax/solid`   | Official Alpha adapter  | signals            |
| `@diax/vanilla` | Official Alpha adapter  | imperative         |

“Official Alpha” means an implementation is maintained in this repository. It does not claim full
parity in rich labels, events, SSR, measurement updates or accessibility until the shared contract
matrix passes.

4\. Mermaid Import [#4-mermaid-import]

DiaX imports a supported Mermaid subset into its normalized AST:

```ts title="mermaid-migration.ts"
import { parseMermaid } from '@diax/mermaid';

const result = parseMermaid(`
  flowchart LR
  A[Start] --> B{Decision}
  B -->|Yes| C[Execute]
`);

if (!result.ast) {
  throw new Error(JSON.stringify(result.diagnostics));
}

console.log(result.diagramType, result.ast.nodes, result.ast.edges);
```

This is an import path, not full Mermaid compatibility. Unsupported families and unsupported syntax
produce diagnostics instead of being guessed or silently rendered as another diagram type.

5\. Size Is a Release Contract [#5-size-is-a-release-contract]

Package size is measured from real build artifacts in CI, including a complete-entry ceiling. We do
not publish a fixed gzip claim here while that budget is still a release gate, and we do not infer
consumer bundle size from source-module tree shaking alone.

6\. Accessible by Design [#6-accessible-by-design]

Diagrams are often a black box for screen readers. DiaX keeps node content as native HTML and emits
valid relationship hints such as `aria-flowto`. It deliberately avoids assigning anonymous group or
button roles to visual-only node wrappers. Those hints do not replace meaningful headings, links,
buttons, text alternatives or keyboard behavior in your node components; the accessibility contract
remains part of the framework test matrix.


# Release Status (/docs/guide/release-status)





Current verdict [#current-verdict]

DiaX is an **unpublished Alpha workspace preview**. The technical foundation is ready for an Alpha
release candidate, but the product is not yet ready for a Beta or production-support promise.

| Question                                  | Current answer                                                                         |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Can I evaluate the real implementation?   | Yes — clone this repository and run its docs, examples and contracts                   |
| Are the packages available on npm?        | No                                                                                     |
| Is there a stable `latest` release?       | No                                                                                     |
| Is production use recommended?            | No                                                                                     |
| Are shadcn registry and v0 actions ready? | No — packages and a public registry URL must ship first                                |
| Is the interface frozen for 1.0?          | No — the candidate surfaces below are still pre-1.0                                    |
| What is the intended first channel?       | `alpha`, with npm provenance after the release gate passes                             |
| What identity is bound today?             | `development` toward `0.1.0`; no release commit, Git tag or artifact digest is claimed |

<Callout type="warn">
  Do not treat an import shown in a code example as evidence that the package is already available
  from npm. Every installation panel intentionally shows the repository workflow until the first
  Alpha is published.
</Callout>

Evaluate the workspace today [#evaluate-the-workspace-today]

Use Node.js `20.19+` or `22.12+` and pnpm `10+`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/diax-labs/diax.git
cd diax
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm docs:dev
```

Open the local URL printed by the docs process. Start with one task rather than the package list:

* [Diagram](/docs/react) when nodes and relations are data and DiaX should own placement;
* [Connect DOM](/docs/react/connect) when JSX, Tailwind or semantic HTML already owns placement;
* [Mermaid Import](/docs/guide/mermaid) when a supported Mermaid document is the source;
* [Markdown & MDX](/docs/guide/mdx-guide) when a build should transform supported fences and report invalid source;
* [AI & Agents](/docs/guide/agent-workflow) when generated output must cross validation, preview and delivery seams;
* [UI Primitives](/docs/ui-react) when you need reusable DOM presentation vocabulary.

The workspace path proves the checked-in implementation and examples. It is not a substitute for a
published tarball or a production support policy.

Interface confidence [#interface-confidence]

Pre-1.0 does not mean every export has equal status. Choose the shallowest interface that completes
your task:

| Tier                       | Recommended surface                                                | Commitment today                                          |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Most React applications    | `FlowDiagram`, `Mindmap` from `@diax/react`                        | Candidate high-level Diagram interface                    |
| Authored React layouts     | `ConnectionSurface`, `connectionTarget` from `@diax/react/connect` | Independent, browser-tested Connect interface             |
| Small static React stories | `DiaxNode`, `DiaxEdge`, `FlowDiagram` from `@diax/react/jsx`       | Alpha authoring syntax over the same definition model     |
| Custom React renderers     | `useDiagram`, `DiagramCanvas`, `DiagramNode`, `DiagramEdges`       | Advanced composition interface                            |
| Core consumers             | `computeLayout`, `validateDiagram`, diagnostics and model types    | Candidate Core workflow                                   |
| Adapter authors            | measurement, namespace, marker and rendering helpers               | Public Alpha compatibility surface                        |
| Experimental               | Core AST builders and `@diax/layout-elk`                           | May change after deletion tests and real adopter feedback |

Connect and JSX are separate package entries rather than `mode` values on a universal component.
Mermaid, ELK, UI presets and Notebook are also opt-in. See [Package Entry Points](/docs/reference/package-entry-points)
for loading, SSR and tree-shaking details.

What Alpha does and does not mean [#what-alpha-does-and-does-not-mean]

**Alpha Go** means the repository has focused evidence for its core algorithms, package artifacts,
loading boundaries, browser behavior and documented golden paths. It is suitable for evaluation,
dogfooding and non-critical prototypes.

**Beta No-Go** means the project still needs:

* reviewable vertical-slice commits and one final checkout verification over that exact history;
* an `alpha` publish, installed-consumer verification and provenance attestation;
* release notes for the current large working tree;
* manual docs acceptance at desktop, 320px, keyboard-only, dark mode and 200% zoom;
* real-user dogfooding against a representative diagram corpus;
* a verified private vulnerability-reporting channel and explicit support expectations.

Breaking changes may occur before 1.0. They must still be intentional: Changesets, migration notes,
package entry contracts and release evidence should describe them rather than silently moving the
interface.

Browser and runtime evidence [#browser-and-runtime-evidence]

The release gate exercises built artifacts in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit where a browser runtime
is required. It also checks server-safe Core paths, Next.js Server Component isolation, hydration,
keyboard and pointer behavior, forced colors, zoom, loading boundaries and selected visual
baselines.

On 2026-08-15 an isolated 813-file candidate with no `dist`, Turbo cache or framework build output
exposed and fixed a release-order bug: `pnpm verify` previously entered artifact checks before a
guaranteed full build. The corrected interface now runs the existing production build gate first.
After a public-registry frozen install, the clean candidate passed the complete gate, including 107
static documentation pages, 112 passing browser documentation contracts with 26 intentional
platform skips, and 11 package tarballs containing 212 checked files. A final checkout verification
is still required after the working tree is split into reviewable commits.

That automation does not replace manual documentation review. The five golden documentation routes
remain pending for desktop, 320px, keyboard, dark mode and 200% zoom until an interactive browser
session is available.

Release policy [#release-policy]

The first public packages must use the `alpha` dist-tag, not `latest`. `pnpm verify` is the single
release interface shared by local development and GitHub Actions. A release is incomplete until all
of these agree:

1. package versions, dependency ranges and Changesets;
2. packed ESM, CJS where declared, types, schemas and CSS;
3. Vite, Webpack, Next.js and Module Federation consumers;
4. browser contracts and documentation contracts;
5. Git tag, GitHub Release, npm dist-tag and provenance;
6. installation instructions shown on this site.

`docs/release-status.json` deliberately separates intent from proof. Development state records the
intended version and dist-tag but keeps release commit, Git tag, content-tree digest and verification
commit empty. A prerelease/release identity is accepted only when all four bind to the current clean
checkout. Changing a shipped input after tagging therefore makes the identity stale instead of
letting two different payloads present themselves as the same release. Generated Agent Skill
artifacts carry the same content-tree and source facts, while their verification status remains
pending until the complete release gate finishes.

The same interface begins with a full-lockfile audit against the public npm registry. High or
Critical findings fail both CI and release; they are not converted into advisory-only output. The
current lockfile had no known registry vulnerabilities on 2026-08-15 after its patched transitive
versions passed package, Storybook, size-budget, and Next production builds. This is point-in-time
dependency evidence—not a substitute for private vulnerability reporting or application-level
trust-boundary review.

After the first Alpha is actually published, the shared release manifest will switch every
installation panel from Workspace Preview to real npm, pnpm, Yarn and Bun commands. shadcn registry
and v0 actions remain hidden until both the packages and the public registry URL are verified.
Until then, a registry install command on this site is a regression.

That first real artifact also starts the compatibility corpus. Maintainers will retain the exact
registry tarballs, the generated Skill artifact and a minimal set of tagged consumer inputs, then
replay those inputs against later packed candidates. The current unpublished workspace deliberately
does not invent a `v1` schema or preserve pre-release defects as historical behavior. See the
[post-Alpha activation checklist](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/blob/main/docs/owner/2026-08-post-alpha-compatibility-corpus.md).

Related owner evidence [#related-owner-evidence]

* [Roadmap](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/blob/main/docs/ROADMAP.md)
* [Release Candidate Interface Freeze](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/blob/main/docs/decisions/035-release-candidate-interface-freeze.md)
* [Release Candidate Consolidation](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/blob/main/docs/owner/2026-07-release-candidate-consolidation.md)
* [Release Security Gate Recovery](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/blob/main/docs/owner/2026-07-release-security-gate.md)
* [Security Policy](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/blob/main/SECURITY.md)


# AI Authoring Context (/docs/guide/skills)





Choose the smallest context source [#choose-the-smallest-context-source]

AI coding assistants already understand JSX, HTML, CSS, Markdown and framework composition. DiaX
context should teach only the product decisions they cannot infer: who owns layout, which package
entry represents the job, how relations are validated, and which presentation roles are trusted.

| Agent task                                      | Give it this context                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Answer questions or inspect an existing project | [`/llms.txt`](/llms.txt) plus the relevant guide                                                 |
| Work offline with the complete documentation    | [`/llms-full.txt`](/llms-full.txt)                                                               |
| Choose and implement one DiaX workflow          | The `skills/diax/SKILL.md` router, then one relevant detail skill                                |
| Generate untrusted runtime output               | The [Agent-first Workflow](/docs/guide/agent-workflow), then the JSON schema and validation loop |
| Author reviewed JSX, MDX or a report            | The [Agent-first Workflow](/docs/guide/agent-workflow), AI Cookbook and relevant framework guide |

<Callout type="warn">
  DiaX is still an unpublished workspace preview. The repository can now compile and verify one
  local, single-router Skill artifact, but no `diax/skills` repository or universal install URL has
  been published. Use the checked-in sources or a locally built artifact from the same commit; do
  not treat installer discovery as a release or model-success claim.
</Callout>

Repository-bundled skills [#repository-bundled-skills]

The canonical, exact-case `SKILL.md` sources live in the
[`skills/` directory](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/tree/main/skills) of this repository:

| Skill           | Use it for                                                                   |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `diax`          | Small task router for layout ownership, trust boundary and package selection |
| `diax-basics`   | Diagram definitions, relation syntax and the Diagram / Connect choice        |
| `diax-react`    | React Diagram, JSX Definition and Connect entries                            |
| `diax-vue`      | Vue components, scoped slots and composables                                 |
| `diax-svelte`   | Svelte components, slots and stores                                          |
| `diax-solid`    | Solid components, render functions and signals                               |
| `diax-vanilla`  | Imperative lifecycle and DOM render callbacks                                |
| `diax-themes`   | Theme values, CSS variables and application-owned theme state                |
| `diax-mermaid`  | Supported Mermaid import, diagnostics and `remark-diax`                      |
| `diax-ui-react` | Mermaid-shaped primitives and semantic Presentation roles                    |
| `diax-advanced` | Namespaces, layout plans, ELK and custom renderers                           |
| `diax-docs`     | Documentation terminology, runnable examples and release truth               |

The repository runs `pnpm smoke:skills` to verify exact entry casing, required frontmatter,
relative references, package subpath exports, removed interface names and current release truth.
This validates the checked-in skill sources; it does not claim that a universal installer or
separately versioned skill package has been published.

Single-router distribution artifact [#single-router-distribution-artifact]

Maintainers can compile the twelve source Skills into one installable artifact. Only `diax` remains
discoverable; the eleven task-specific Skills become routed `references/*.md` files so an agent does
not install or load them all as peers.

```bash
node scripts/build-agent-skill.mjs --output /an/empty/output/diax-skill
npx --yes skills@1.5.22 add /an/empty/output/diax-skill --list --full-depth
```

The compiler refuses an existing output directory, stages only an explicit source allowlist, and
records every payload SHA-256 plus package entries, release truth, adapter capabilities, source
commit, dirty state and untracked inputs. It also embeds the generated question-first scenario
corpus so a user question can select one checked recipe without loading the complete Showcase.
Offline smoke verifies exactly one `SKILL.md`, all routed references, schema/resources, manifest
containment and byte-identical rebuilds. The optional
installer smoke pins `skills@1.5.22` and must report exactly one `diax` Skill.

Generated artifacts remain `releaseEligible: false`. Publication still requires the real-model
attempt-one matrix and identified human review; a clean artifact and a successful installer scan do
not prove that an ordinary model produced a useful visual.

Maintainer evaluation status [#maintainer-evaluation-status]

DiaX now includes a provider-neutral, six-case attempt-one benchmark for Diagram JSON, Connect TSX,
Mermaid import, trusted MDX, dense layout and Presentation roles. It freezes the prompt, routed
Skills, public package-entry hashes and the first candidate, then produces a deterministic receipt.

This is maintainer tooling, not a published success-rate claim. Fast runs use workspace entries;
reviewable runs can now freeze and install real package tarballs in an isolated consumer with
`--qualification packed-artifact`, then render the exact candidate with the isolated `browser`
command. A private provider-neutral `capture` command accepts the untouched external output once or
records a provider/no-candidate failure log; it does not call a provider or make a fixture into model
evidence. Receipts say `modelExecution: not-recorded` when that intake was not used. No ordinary-model
result matrix has been published. The checked-in browser fixtures and
their automated screenshots do not replace an identified human visual reviewer. The browser
evidence also freezes an ARIA snapshot and checks DOM-id/`aria-flowto` integrity. Chromium exercises
forced-colors and reduced-motion emulation; Firefox and WebKit cross a representative packed route.
These are automated preflights, not screen-reader, Windows High Contrast or hardware Safari results.
See the
[`ordinary-model-floor` protocol](https://github.com/diax-labs/diax/tree/main/benchmarks/ordinary-model-floor)
for the exact evidence boundary.

Clone or download the repository, start with `skills/diax/SKILL.md`, then copy only the routed detail
skill into the project-instruction location supported by your coding assistant. Do not install all
skills globally by default: narrower context makes package and layout ownership easier for an agent
to preserve.

AI-safe Diagram output [#ai-safe-diagram-output]

For untrusted runtime generation, ask for serializable Diagram data—not JSX. A minimal output looks
like this:

```json title="AI-generated Diagram Definition"
{
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "browser", "content": "Browser" },
    { "id": "api", "content": "API" },
    { "id": "database", "content": "Database" }
  ],
  "relations": [
    { "from": "browser", "to": "api", "label": "HTTPS" },
    { "from": "api", "to": "database", "label": "SQL" }
  ]
}
```

This is an example value, not a hand-written substitute for the schema. Resolve the published
workspace schema from `diax/schemas/diax.json`, validate its structure, then run
`validateDiagram()` before rendering. Preserve diagnostic `code`, `path`, `message` and `hint` when
asking the model to repair invalid output.

Task classification prompt [#task-classification-prompt]

Give an agent the ownership decision before asking it to write code:

If the request starts from a communication question rather than a package name, match it against
the question-first recipes in the [AI Cookbook](/docs/guide/ai-cookbook), then load only the selected
task context.

1. Use **Diagram** when nodes and relations are data and DiaX should place them.
2. Use **Connect** when reviewed JSX, Tailwind or semantic HTML already owns placement.
3. Use **Mermaid Import** only when Mermaid text is the source; do not make every Diagram consumer
   load the parser.
4. Use `@diax/ui-react/presentation` when the reader needs stable semantic roles such as actor,
   system, artifact, metric, evidence, decision, risk or data store.
5. Keep relations centralized. Do not invent a universal `mode`, duplicate topology inside node
   components, or expose routing waypoints to generated output.

For a concrete engineering output, distinguish all three surrounding meanings:

* `SystemNode` is the producer or consumer that performs work.
* `ArtifactNode` is one versioned output moving between systems.
* `DataStoreNode` is the registry or durable collection that stores many outputs.

Trust boundary [#trust-boundary]

Reviewed source code may use JSX, MDX and application components because a human and the normal
build pipeline remain in the loop. Untrusted model output should stay schema-validated data mapped
through an allowlisted renderer registry. Do not compile arbitrary model-produced JSX in the
browser.

Keep context current [#keep-context-current]

Package entry points and maturity can change before 1.0. Prefer this documentation site's
`/llms.txt`, the checked-in skills from the same commit, and the
[Release Status](/docs/guide/release-status) page over copied prompts from an older version.

Next steps [#next-steps]

* [Agent-first Workflow](/docs/guide/agent-workflow) — one bounded path from question to delivered artifact
* [AI integration](/docs/guide/ai-integration) — schema, validation, diagnostics and repair
* [AI Cookbook](/docs/guide/ai-cookbook) — Diagram and Connect choices for real visual stories
* [Presentation Nodes](/docs/ui-react/presentation-nodes) — trusted semantic DOM vocabulary
* [Package Entry Points](/docs/reference/package-entry-points) — loading and runtime boundaries
* [MDX Guide](/docs/guide/mdx-guide) — reviewed Markdown/MDX authoring and `remark-diax`


# Themes (/docs/guide/themes)





Overview [#overview]

DiaX uses CSS custom properties (variables) for theming. The `DefaultNodeRenderer` in `<FlowDiagram>` reads these variables, so you can customize the entire look by setting CSS variables on a parent element, or simply pass the `theme` prop.

Built-in Themes [#built-in-themes]

| Theme    | Description                               | Best for                        |
| -------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `linear` | Dark, Linear-inspired aesthetic (default) | Dark backgrounds, presentations |
| `light`  | Clean light theme                         | Light backgrounds, docs         |
| `notion` | Simple black & white                      | Notion-style pages              |
| `github` | GitHub Actions workflow style             | GitHub-adjacent contexts        |

  code="`<FlowDiagram

  { id: 'a', content: 'Design' },

  { id: 'c', content: 'Ship' },
]}
relations={['a->b', 'b->c']}
centered density=&#x22;spacious&#x22;
/>`"

  <FlowDiagram

    { id: 'a', content: 'Design' },

Usage [#usage]

With Theme Presets [#with-theme-presets]

```tsx
import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

// Recommended: use the theme prop directly
<FlowDiagram theme="light" nodes={nodes} relations={relations} />;
```

```tsx
// Notion theme
<FlowDiagram
  nodes={nodes}
  relations={relations}
  theme="notion"
  density="spacious"
/>

// GitHub theme
<FlowDiagram
  nodes={nodes}
  relations={relations}
  theme="github"
  density="spacious"
/>
```

Or generate CSS:

```ts
import { themes, themeToCSS } from 'diax/themes';
const css = themeToCSS(themes.light, '.my-diagram');
```

CSS Variables Reference [#css-variables-reference]

| Variable              | Default (linear)                 | Description      |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| `--diax-font`         | `"Inter", system-ui, sans-serif` | Font family      |
| `--diax-node-bg`      | `linear-gradient(...)`           | Node background  |
| `--diax-node-text`    | `#EDEDEF`                        | Node text color  |
| `--diax-node-border`  | `rgba(255,255,255,0.08)`         | Node border      |
| `--diax-node-shadow`  | `0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.3)...`   | Node shadow      |
| `--diax-edge-color`   | `currentColor`                   | Edge stroke      |
| `--diax-label-text`   | `#8A8F98`                        | Label text       |
| `--diax-label-bg`     | `#0a0a0c`                        | Label background |
| `--diax-label-border` | `rgba(255,255,255,0.06)`         | Label border     |
| `--diax-accent`       | `#5E6AD2`                        | Accent color     |

Custom Themes [#custom-themes]

A custom theme is a visual contract, not only a node palette. Always set an edge color and the label
canvas it must sit on for both color schemes. DiaX cannot infer a readable stroke from a brand color;
the maintainer and browser contracts target at least `3:1` edge-to-label-canvas contrast. If your host
uses a different canvas behind the SVG, check that pair too.

```ts title="custom-theme.ts"
import type { DiaxTheme } from 'diax/themes';

const myTheme: DiaxTheme = {
  name: 'my-brand',
  light: {
    '--diax-node-bg': '#ffffff',
    '--diax-node-text': '#111827',
    '--diax-edge-color': '#334155',
    '--diax-label-bg': '#ffffff',
  },
  dark: {
    '--diax-node-bg': '#111827',
    '--diax-node-text': '#f9fafb',
    '--diax-edge-color': '#e2e8f0',
    '--diax-label-bg': '#0f172a',
  },
};
```

Do not use a translucent white edge as a dark-mode fallback. It can be geometrically present while
becoming indistinguishable from a light host surface. Verify the result in the real browser after
fonts and rich labels settle, especially when `highlightOnHover` dims unrelated edges.

Pass the value directly—custom names are not stored in global mutable state:

```tsx
<FlowDiagram
  theme={myTheme}
  nodes={nodes}
  relations={relations}
/>
```

For manual DOM integration, resolve and inject explicitly:

```ts
import { injectThemeStyles, resolveTheme } from 'diax/themes';

const theme = resolveTheme('github');
if (theme) {
  injectThemeStyles(theme);
  container.dataset.diaxTheme = theme.name;
}
```

The framework adapters perform this step automatically when you pass a `theme` prop.

Dark Mode Toggle [#dark-mode-toggle]

```css title="globals.css"
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --diax-node-bg: linear-gradient(
      to bottom,
      rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06),
      rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.02)
    );
    --diax-node-text: #ededef;
  }
}
```
