  <Card title="API Reference" href="/docs/reference" description="themes, resolveTheme, and CSS conversion" />
</Cards>


# Troubleshooting (/docs/guide/troubleshooting)



1\. Nodes Render but Edges Don't Appear [#1-nodes-render-but-edges-dont-appear]

**Cause**: The framework has not successfully passed DOM identifiers, or SVG container styles are misplaced.

**Solution**:
If building headless without the built-in component wrapper, check the following:

* Are you spreading `bindProps` correctly at the ROOT of each wrapper item for `data-diax-node` injection?
* Without `data-diax-node={id}`, the resize observer CANNOT map elements to the graph engine!

```tsx
// INCORRECT ❌
<div><div {...node.bindProps}>{node.content}</div></div> // [!code --]

// CORRECT ✅
<div {...node.bindProps}><div>{node.content}</div></div> // [!code ++]
```

2\. Edges Are Floating Inside My Node [#2-edges-are-floating-inside-my-node]

**Cause**: By default, edges wrap to the bounding border box. If you set margins or paddings on the root `<div {...bindProps}>`, DiaX reads those as part of the total DOM width.

**Solution**: Only apply inner-content padding on a child `div` wrapped inside the bound element.

3\. Hydration Error or Missing SSR Output [#3-hydration-error-or-missing-ssr-output]

**Cause**: The server and first client render received different topology/content, the application
read browser-only state during render, or the bundler selected the wrong framework package
condition. DOM measurement itself is deferred until mount and should not require removing SSR.

**Solution**:

* keep the first nodes, relations, IDs and rendered content deterministic;
* in Next.js, import `@diax/react` from a Client Component and pass JSON-safe data across RSC;
* for Solid and Svelte, let the resolver choose the package's server/browser or Svelte conditions;
* for Vue, preserve the SSR shell and start application browser SDKs after mount;
* use `ClientOnly`, `ssr: false`, or route-level SSR disablement only when application-owned content
  is intentionally browser-only.

Final pixel paths appear after hydration; that is expected and is different from a hydration error.
See [Framework Parity](/docs/guide/feature-parity) and the adapter's SSR page for current evidence.

4\. Edge Animations Not Playing [#4-edge-animations-not-playing]

**Cause**: The `injectEdgeStyles()` function hasn't been called, or your bundler is tree-shaking it away.

**Solution**: The built-in `<FlowDiagram>` and `<Mindmap>` components call this automatically. If you're using the headless `useDiagram()` hook with a custom SVG renderer, ensure `injectEdgeStyles()` is called once at mount:

```tsx
import { injectEdgeStyles } from 'diax';

useEffect(() => {
  injectEdgeStyles();
}, []);
```

5\. Theme Not Applying / CSS Variables Not Set [#5-theme-not-applying--css-variables-not-set]

**Cause**: Manual theme integration requires both `injectThemeStyles()` from `diax/themes` and the correct `data-diax-theme` attribute.

**Solution**: Use the built-in `<FlowDiagram theme="notion">` which handles this automatically. For headless usage, call `injectThemeStyles(theme)` and set the `data-diax-theme` attribute on the container.

6\. Stagger Animation Not Working [#6-stagger-animation-not-working]

**Cause**: Stagger mode changes the `measureMode` internally to `"auto"`. If you've overridden `measureMode` to `"resize"`, stagger columns won't re-measure correctly.

**Solution**: Let DiaX auto-select `measureMode` when using stagger, or explicitly set `measureMode="auto"`.

7\. ResizeObserver Loop Error in Console [#7-resizeobserver-loop-error-in-console]

**Cause**: A `ResizeObserver` callback, in DiaX or host code, wrote layout-affecting state while the
browser was still delivering resize notifications. The resulting size change could not be delivered
in the same update cycle. Treat the warning as a scheduling defect until the producer is identified;
filtering it can hide stale edge or label geometry.

**Solution**:

* reproduce it with the exact framework, browser and rich DOM content;
* keep observer callbacks read-only, deduplicate equal measurements and commit layout state in a
  later animation frame;
* disconnect observers and cancel pending frames when the diagram unmounts;
* if the warning remains with a current DiaX release, capture the smallest fixture and browser name
  in a bug report instead of filtering the console event.

Official adapter browser contracts enlarge and restore rich labels in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit
and fail when this warning is emitted.

8\. Experimental ELK Layout Does Not Complete [#8-experimental-elk-layout-does-not-complete]

**Cause**: `elkLayout().computeLayoutPlan()` is asynchronous. A large graph may be expensive, and a
deployment that moves ELK to a Worker must allow that worker in its CSP.

**Solution**:

* catch and render errors from the returned Promise;
* add an application timeout for user-supplied or unbounded graphs;
* if your application runs ELK in a Worker, verify the Worker CSP and deployment URL;
* pass the resulting plan to React `DiagramEdges`, or consume it with
  `computeEdgePathsFromLayoutPlan` in a custom renderer;
* use legacy `computeLayout()` only when intentionally accepting lossy grid quantization.

9\. Mermaid Syntax Parsing Fails [#9-mermaid-syntax-parsing-fails]

**Cause**: `parseMermaid()` from `@diax/mermaid` recognizes six diagram families, but implements a
documented subset of each family's syntax. Mermaid directives such as click handlers, styling and
unsupported constructs are not executed or silently approximated.

**Solution**: Inspect the returned `diagnostics`; render only when `result.ast` is non-null. If the
source relies on an unsupported family or feature, render it with Mermaid itself or rewrite that
part using DiaX's typed topology and DOM renderers. See the [Mermaid guide](/docs/guide/mermaid) for
the supported subset and fidelity limits.

The DiaX Playground applies this policy directly: JSON mode checks definition structure and Core
graph diagnostics before rendering, while Mermaid mode preserves the importer's source location and
hint. The error panel names the exact subject and offers one supported next edit. It deliberately
does not suggest bend points, coordinates, or a multi-step automatic rewrite.

10\. TypeScript Errors After Upgrade [#10-typescript-errors-after-upgrade]

**Cause**: DiaX uses strict TypeScript with `readonly` modifiers on output interfaces (`ComputedEdgePath`, `HighlightResult`, etc.). If you're mutating these objects, TS will report errors.

**Solution**: Clone the object before mutating:

```ts
import { computeEdgePaths } from 'diax/layout-plan';

// INCORRECT ❌
const path = computeEdgePaths(edges, rects, layoutMap)[0];
path.labelX = 100; // Error: readonly property // [!code --]

// CORRECT ✅
const path = { ...computeEdgePaths(edges, rects, layoutMap)[0], labelX: 100 }; // [!code ++]
```

11\. Bundle Size Larger Than Expected [#11-bundle-size-larger-than-expected]

**Cause**: Importing `@diax/mermaid`, `@diax/ui-react/mermaid`, or a product surface such as
`@diax/notebook` adds capability-specific dependencies.

**Solution**: The core `diax` package has no runtime dependencies. Run `pnpm size:check` in the repository for current build-artifact measurements.
For minimal bundles:

* Import only what you need: `import { computeLayout } from 'diax'`
* Import measured automatic routing from `diax/layout-plan`; use `diax/edge-geometry` for authored DOM placement
* Import DOM presets from `@diax/ui-react`; use `/mermaid` only when text parsing is required
* Lazy-load `@diax/ui-react/mermaid` when Mermaid is an optional user-selected mode
* Check your bundler's output with `pnpm size` to verify


# Visual Constitution (/docs/guide/visual-constitution)



DiaX is infrastructure for visual explanation. Its most characteristic material is not a glow,
gradient or card shape: it is a legible relationship between real DOM artifacts. This constitution
governs the README, documentation site, Showcase, Playground and DiaX-owned UI recipes. It does not
govern an application's brand and it is not a theme preset.

<Callout type="info">
  **The host owns visual identity. DiaX-owned surfaces make structure, evidence and state easier to
  read.**
</Callout>

The seven rules [#the-seven-rules]

1\. Respect the host [#1-respect-the-host]

DOM-native content should inherit the host's typography, spacing, color scheme and component
language. Defaults must be calm enough to compose with an existing design system. DiaX must not
impose a terminal, neon, mono-everywhere, dark-first or "AI dashboard" identity on consumer content.

2\. Put the reading path first [#2-put-the-reading-path-first]

The title, primary claim, supporting evidence and next action form the page before decoration does.
Node meaning must remain understandable when arrows are unavailable; relation meaning needs a text,
semantic or accessible counterpart when the connector carries essential information. Hover, focus,
motion and color may reinforce that path, but cannot create the only path.

3\. Spend visual emphasis on meaning [#3-spend-visual-emphasis-on-meaning]

Saturated color identifies a state, category, risk, decision or active path. A border separates
materials. Radius groups a coherent surface. Shadow indicates elevation or overlap. If an effect
does not explain hierarchy, state or material, remove it.

This is intentionally stricter than "make every card consistent." A comparison table, architecture
map, evidence trail and roadmap do different communication jobs and may require different visual
grammars.

4\. Design for the final use size [#4-design-for-the-final-use-size]

A gallery thumbnail and a reading viewport have different contracts:

| Context     | It must prove                                                                                           | It does not prove                                |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Thumbnail   | Subject, broad composition, main regions and direction are recognizable                                 | Body copy and edge labels are readable           |
| Reading     | Prose, metadata, node labels, edge labels, controls and focus state are usable at the intended viewport | The same result will survive print or projection |
| Destination | The exported file remains legible in its actual slide, page, screen or print context                    | Every other destination is accepted              |

Do not shrink a complete report until it technically fits a card and call that success. Use the
thumbnail to select a story; use the detail page, Playground or host viewport to read it.

5\. Keep interaction optional [#5-keep-interaction-optional]

Pointer hover can reveal detail, but the same detail needs a keyboard and touch path. Motion can
clarify a state transition, but reduced motion must preserve the result. Deleting animation should
leave a coherent static composition. Canonical controls and content must not disappear only because
the pointer is elsewhere.

6\. Let recipes remain plural [#6-let-recipes-remain-plural]

Showcase and `@diax/ui-react` demonstrate vocabulary, not one house skin. Reuse semantic roles when
their meaning is stable; vary composition, density, typography and material according to the story.
Do not turn every recipe into a rounded grid of glowing cards. A new Presentation role still needs
two independent real scenarios; a new visual treatment does not justify a new public component.

7\. Name the evidence boundary [#7-name-the-evidence-boundary]

Automated checks prove only their named facts. A screenshot diff can prove pixel stability in its
captured engine and viewport. It cannot claim taste, screen-reader comprehension, Windows High
Contrast, hardware Safari, projector legibility or print quality. Those require the stated target
environment and, where appropriate, an identified human reviewer.

Obligations by surface [#obligations-by-surface]

| DiaX-owned surface | Primary job                                  | Review obligation                                                                                                               |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| README             | Explain the thesis and earn first trust      | Use a real artifact, current release truth and a short path to first success; avoid unverifiable adoption or performance claims |
| Docs               | Get a user to a working result               | Task-first navigation, complete contracts where promised, visible results and honest maturity/runtime labels                    |
| Showcase           | Help a reader choose a communication pattern | Preserve visual variety, label thumbnail versus reading evidence and provide a readable detail path                             |
| Playground         | Turn source into a reviewable artifact       | Keep editing, diagnostics, preview state and export truth clearer than ambient decoration                                       |
| `@diax/ui-react`   | Supply composable semantic DOM vocabulary    | Encode role and material without owning the page skin; keep optional leaves and host styling boundaries intact                  |

Wide Showcase studies may provide a semantic overview beside the Guided Study controls. It is a
viewer-only projection of final DOM target rectangles and the real scroll viewport: it does not
reconstruct edge topology, enter canonical export or become a Core minimap. The overview belongs in
normal document flow so chapter controls, legends and navigation cannot overlap by accident. It
must expose keyboard and pointer navigation, stable target names, reduced-motion and forced-colors
behavior, and disappear when the study has no genuine horizontal reading canvas.

The subtractive review [#the-subtractive-review]

Before accepting a DiaX-owned visual, review the real viewport and ask:

1. What is the first sentence, object or path the reader should understand?
2. If color, animation and hover disappear, what meaning disappears with them?
3. Does every saturated color, border, radius and shadow explain something?
4. Is this a thumbnail or a reading context, and are we testing the correct promise?
5. Does the design inherit from its host, or does it look like a detached generated dashboard?
6. Does the recipe solve this communication job differently for a reason?
7. Which claims are automated evidence, and which still need human or hardware acceptance?

If the answer relies on one more decorative layer, remove that layer and strengthen the information
structure instead.

Related contracts [#related-contracts]

* [Accessibility](/docs/guide/accessibility) — semantics, keyboard behavior and assistive-technology evidence
* [Export DOM Visuals](/docs/guide/exporting) — destination-specific capture and review truth
* [Presentation Nodes](/docs/ui-react/presentation-nodes) — semantic DOM vocabulary
* [Presentation Recipes](/docs/ui-react/presentation-recipes) — composed communication patterns
* [Release Status](/docs/guide/release-status) — what current automation and manual review can claim


# Advanced (/docs/react/advanced)



DOM Namespaces [#dom-namespaces]

Use `namespace` to prevent DOM ID collisions when multiple diagrams render on the same page. Edges between nodes inside each diagram continue to use local IDs:

```tsx
<div className="flex gap-8">
  <FlowDiagram
    namespace="fe"
    nodes={frontendNodes}
    relations={['gw->bff']}
  />
  <FlowDiagram namespace="be" nodes={backendNodes} relations={['svc->db']} />
</div>
```

Node IDs become `namespace::nodeId` in the DOM, while relations inside a diagram keep using local IDs such as `gw->bff`.

<Callout type="warn">
  Built-in renderers currently measure and draw edges inside one diagram container. A relation such as `bff->be::svc` is preserved as a cross-diagram reference, but it is not drawn across the two containers. Use one diagram for the connected graph, or provide your own shared measurement and SVG overlay.
</Callout>

***

Node Type Registry (`nodeTypes`) [#node-type-registry-nodetypes]

Define reusable node renderers by type, then reference them in the nodes array:

```tsx
const nodeTypes = {
  gateway: (node, state) => (
    <div className="px-5 py-3 rounded-xl bg-indigo-500/10 border border-indigo-500/20 text-indigo-300">
      ⬡ {node.content}
    </div>
  ),
  service: (node, state) => (
    <div className="px-4 py-2 rounded-lg bg-emerald-500/10 border border-emerald-500/20 text-emerald-300">
      ● {node.content}
    </div>
  ),
};

<FlowDiagram
  nodes={[
    { id: 'gw', type: 'gateway', content: 'API Gateway' },
    { id: 'auth', type: 'service', content: 'Auth Service' },
    { id: 'user', type: 'service', content: 'User Service' },
  ]}
  relations={['gw->auth', 'gw->user']}
  nodeTypes={nodeTypes}
/>;
```

**Resolution order**: `renderNode` > `nodeTypes[node.type]` > default renderer.


# Connect Authored DOM (/docs/react/connect)





Keep your layout, add connections [#keep-your-layout-add-connections]

Use Connect when the page already has the right layout and DiaX should only draw relationships. Your
grid, flexbox, responsive breakpoints and semantic elements remain ordinary application DOM.

| Use Diagram when…                                         | Use Connect when…                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| You have nodes and relations and want automatic placement | You already have a report, article, dashboard or application layout |
| DiaX should own grid placement                            | Your CSS should remain the layout authority                         |
| One graph model drives the whole surface                  | Connections annotate selected elements inside richer content        |

Connect is a separate React entry so Diagram-only consumers do not evaluate its measurement runtime:

```tsx
import { ConnectionSurface, connectionTarget } from '@diax/react/connect';
```

<Callout type="info">
  Connect is currently available for React. Vue, Svelte, Solid and Vanilla adapters continue to
  support automatic Diagram layout but do not yet expose this authored-DOM surface.
</Callout>

Quick start [#quick-start]

```tsx title="decision-report.tsx" contract
'use client';

import type { DiaxRelation } from '@diax/react';
import { ConnectionSurface, connectionTarget } from '@diax/react/connect';

const relations = [
  {
    from: 'brief',
    to: 'decision',
    label: 'approved',
    sourceAnchor: 'right',
    targetAnchor: 'left',
    pathType: 'orthogonal',
  },
] satisfies DiaxRelation[];

export function DecisionReport() {
  return (
    <ConnectionSurface
      relations={relations}
      className="grid gap-16 md:grid-cols-2"
    >
      <section {...connectionTarget('brief')} className="rounded-2xl border p-6">
        <p className="text-sm text-slate-500">AI brief</p>
        <h2 className="text-xl font-semibold">Adopt the new checkout</h2>
      </section>

      <article
        {...connectionTarget('decision')}
        className="rounded-2xl bg-emerald-50 p-6"
      >
        <p className="text-sm text-emerald-700">Decision</p>
        <strong>Approved for staged rollout</strong>
      </article>
    </ConnectionSurface>
  );
}
```

`connectionTarget(id)` returns a small attribute object. Spread it onto the exact element whose border
box should become the connection endpoint. A custom component must forward that object to one real
DOM element rather than swallowing it.

Inspect Runnable Connect Studies [#inspect-runnable-connect-studies]

These studies keep layout in semantic JSX and CSS while Connect measures only the marked endpoints.
Open a study to inspect its ownership contract, live DOM, generated registry artifact and source.

<ShowcaseStudies
  slugs="[
  'dom-system-architecture',
  'incident-response-workflow',
  'snapshot-fan-in',
  'agent-review-sequence',
]"
/>

Sequence-style protocols without a Sequence mode [#sequence-style-protocols-without-a-sequence-mode]

A chronological protocol is a good Connect composition when the application owns participant
columns and message order. Give every message row one tiny endpoint under its sender and one under
its receiver, then connect those measured elements with a stable relation ID:

```tsx title="message-row.tsx"
const message = { id: 'm03-review', from: 'verifier', to: 'agent' };

<div className="grid grid-cols-3" data-message={message.id}>
  {participants.map(participant => {
    const endpoint = participant.id === message.from || participant.id === message.to;
    return (
      <div key={participant.id} className="relative min-h-16">
        {endpoint ? (
          <span
            {...connectionTarget(`${message.id}-${participant.id}`)}
            aria-hidden="true"
          />
        ) : null}
      </div>
    );
  })}
</div>
```

The corresponding relation connects `${message.id}-${message.from}` to
`${message.id}-${message.to}` with `pathType: 'straight'`. The row owns chronology; Connect only owns
the exact line between its endpoints. This avoids public `y`, `messageAt`, lifeline-port or channel
coordinates and remains stable when typography changes.

At narrow widths, do not shrink a four- or five-participant trace until its text is illegible. Make
an ordered semantic transcript the primary presentation, as the
[Agent Review Sequence](/showcase/agent-review-sequence) does. The desktop trace and compact
transcript express the same messages; CSS chooses the readable representation.

Topology stays centralized [#topology-stays-centralized]

Keep relations next to the surface rather than hiding them inside target components. This makes the
story reviewable by people, TypeScript and AI tooling:

```tsx
const relations = [
  { from: 'claim', to: 'evidence', label: 'because' },
  { from: 'evidence', to: 'decision', style: 'dashed' },
];

<ConnectionSurface relations={relations}>
  <p {...connectionTarget('claim')}>Conversion improved after the rollout.</p>
  <MetricCard {...connectionTarget('evidence')} value="+23%" />
  <aside {...connectionTarget('decision')}>Expand to the remaining regions.</aside>
</ConnectionSurface>;
```

The same rich relation model used by Diagram is available here, including labels, markers, anchors,
path types, animation, stroke styling, hit slop and edge events. Prefer object-form relations when an
AI or external system generates the topology; explicit fields are easier to validate and repair.

When several automatic relations share one inferred node side, Connect spreads their attachment
points deterministically toward their opposite nodes instead of stacking every line at the side
midpoint. Give dynamic or parallel relations stable `id` values so their slots survive relation
reordering. An explicit `sourceAnchor` or `targetAnchor` remains authoritative and keeps that endpoint
at the selected side midpoint; there is no port-index, channel or bend-point option to maintain.

Surface contract [#surface-contract]

`ConnectionSurface` [#connectionsurface]

| Prop            | Type                                     | Default    | Purpose                                                          |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `relations`     | `readonly DiaxRelation<ReactNode>[]`     | required   | Centralized topology for targets in this surface                 |
| `children`      | `ReactNode`                              | required   | Application-owned semantic DOM                                   |
| `pathType`      | `'bezier' \| 'straight' \| 'orthogonal'` | `'bezier'` | Surface fallback; an individual relation may override it         |
| `onDiagnostics` | `(diagnostics) => void`                  | —          | Receive structured validation results after targets are measured |

The component also accepts normal `div` props such as `className`, `style`, event handlers and a
forwarded `ref`. Connect supplies zero-specificity `position: relative` and `isolation: isolate`
defaults so the SVG layers have a stable containing block and local stacking context. Any host class
or inline style can replace those defaults. Visible relation paint sits behind authored DOM, while a
separate transparent interaction layer keeps actionable edges clickable and keyboard focusable. You
should not need edge-layer `z-index` selectors or a `z-10` class on every target.

This paint ownership does not wrap, clone or reposition children, so direct-child Grid and Flex
semantics remain unchanged. Opaque authored content naturally covers a route. Transparent content
reveals it. If application CSS replaces the surface's `position` or `isolation`, the application also
owns the resulting containing-block and stacking behavior.

`connectionTarget(id)` [#connectiontargetid]

```ts
function connectionTarget(id: string): {
  readonly 'data-diax-node': string;
};
```

IDs must be stable, non-empty and unique inside the nearest surface. Relations use those local IDs;
namespaced cross-surface references such as `report::claim` are intentionally rejected.

Measurement and responsive layout [#measurement-and-responsive-layout]

Connect performs an initial measurement and observes target size, DOM mutations, CSS transitions and
animations. Responsive reflow, images, web fonts and content changes therefore update edge geometry
without a public `refresh()` method.

An intentionally hidden responsive branch is treated as temporarily unmeasurable and emits no edge
geometry for that observer frame. When the branch becomes laid out, normal observation resumes and
finite paths are produced automatically.

```tsx
<ConnectionSurface
  relations={relations}
  className="grid gap-20 lg:grid-cols-[1fr_18rem]"
>
  <main {...connectionTarget('story')}>{children}</main>
  <aside {...connectionTarget('context')} className="lg:sticky lg:top-24">
    Supporting context
  </aside>
</ConnectionSurface>
```

The observer runs a frame loop only while authored CSS motion is active and performs a final
measurement when motion ends. Prefer transform and opacity for visual motion, respect
`prefers-reduced-motion`, and avoid continuously animating large numbers of targets without a user
benefit.

Diagnostics [#diagnostics]

Invalid relations are omitted from the rendered edge layer and reported as structured diagnostics:

```tsx
<ConnectionSurface
  relations={relations}
  onDiagnostics={(diagnostics) => {
    for (const diagnostic of diagnostics) {
      console.warn(diagnostic.code, diagnostic.path, diagnostic.hint);
    }
  }}
>
  {content}
</ConnectionSurface>
```

| Code                        | Meaning                                                  |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `INVALID_NODE_ID`           | A target ID is empty or only whitespace                  |
| `DUPLICATE_NODE_ID`         | Two targets in the same surface use one ID               |
| `MALFORMED_RELATION`        | A relation cannot be parsed                              |
| `ORPHAN_RELATION`           | A relation endpoint does not exist in this surface       |
| `SELF_LOOP`                 | A target connects to itself; rendered with a warning     |
| `UNSUPPORTED_CROSS_SURFACE` | A relation attempts to cross surface or portal ownership |

Diagnostics are data, not console-only warnings. Show them in an authoring UI or feed them back into
an AI repair loop when relations are generated.

Ownership boundaries [#ownership-boundaries]

* The nearest `ConnectionSurface` owns each target. Nested surfaces are isolated.
* Both endpoints must be descendants of the same surface.
* Portals and edges between separate surfaces are not supported.
* Connect does not move, wrap or clone target elements.
* The SVG paint and interaction layers remain presentation; target content retains its native
  semantic HTML.
* Interactive edges need an explicit `ariaLabel` when the fallback endpoint description is not enough.

<Callout type="warn">
  Do not wrap an entire application in one global surface to simulate cross-page connections. Keep a
  surface aligned with one understandable visual composition and keep both endpoints inside it.
</Callout>

Next steps [#next-steps]

* [Edge types and rich relation fields](/docs/guide/edge-types)
* [Accessibility](/docs/guide/accessibility)
* [AI-generated topology](/docs/guide/ai-integration)
* [Automatic Diagram layout](/docs/react)


# Custom Rendering (/docs/react/custom-rendering)



Custom Rendering [#custom-rendering]

Use `renderNode` to customize how nodes look while keeping all layout logic:

```tsx
import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

<FlowDiagram
  nodes={nodes}
  relations={relations}
  renderNode={(node, state) => (
    <div
      className={cn(
        'px-4 py-2 rounded-xl border',
        state === 'highlighted' && 'ring-2 ring-blue-500',
        state === 'dimmed' && 'opacity-25',
      )}
    >
      {node.content}
    </div>
  )}
/>;
```

TypeScript and structured domain data [#typescript-and-structured-domain-data]

`FlowDiagram` accepts renderable React content directly; it is not a generic JSX component. When
nodes carry structured domain objects, use the typed `useDiagram<NodeContent, EdgeLabel,
GroupLabel>()` seam and compose `DiagramCanvas`, `DiagramNode`, and `DiagramEdges`. This keeps the
high-level component simple while preserving strict payload types for custom renderers. See
[Headless Hooks](/docs/react/hooks#independent-payload-types).

Node States [#node-states]

The `state` parameter in `renderNode` tells you the current interaction state:

| State           | When              | Suggested style  |
| --------------- | ----------------- | ---------------- |
| `undefined`     | Default           | Normal           |
| `"highlighted"` | On hover path     | Ring/glow effect |
| `"dimmed"`      | Not on hover path | Reduced opacity  |

Stagger Animation [#stagger-animation]

```tsx
<FlowDiagram stagger />        // Default 120ms delay between layers
<FlowDiagram stagger={200} />  // Custom 200ms delay
```


# Edge Types (/docs/react/edges)



Edge Types [#edge-types]

String DSL [#string-dsl]

```tsx
relations={[
  'a->b',           // Solid arrow
  'a-->b',          // Dashed arrow
  'a<->b',          // Bidirectional
  'a->|label|b',    // With label
]}
```

Object Form [#object-form]

```tsx
relations={[
  { from: 'a', to: 'b', style: 'dashed', color: '#E91E63' },
  { from: 'b', to: 'c', animate: 'flow', label: 'next' },
  { from: 'c', to: 'd', bidirectional: true },
]}
```

Animation Presets [#animation-presets]

| Preset              | Effect                         |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `"flow"`            | Flowing dashes along the edge  |
| `"pulse"`           | Breathing opacity effect       |
| `"shimmer"`         | Light traveling along the edge |
| `"reverse-flow"`    | Reverse flowing dashes         |
| `"reverse-shimmer"` | Reverse shimmer                |

***

Custom Edge Labels [#custom-edge-labels]

Use `renderEdgeLabel` to customize how edge labels are rendered:

```tsx
<FlowDiagram
  nodes={nodes}
  relations={['client->|REST|api', 'api->|SQL|db']}
  renderEdgeLabel={(
    label, // [!code highlight]
  ) => (
    <span className="px-2 py-0.5 rounded-full bg-indigo-500/20 text-indigo-300 text-xs font-mono">
      {label}
    </span>
  )}
/>
```

`FlowDiagram` measures the rendered label and automatically reserves room for it on the primary
layout axis. Text, badges, icons, and dynamic React content therefore do not require a guessed
`gap` or `labelWidth`. The selected density remains the minimum spacing.

This behavior belongs to Diagram because DiaX owns its CSS Grid. In
[Connect](/docs/react/connect), your CSS owns placement, so edge labels do not silently reflow the
authored DOM.

***

Edge Path Types [#edge-path-types]

Control how edges are drawn with the `pathType` prop:

Bezier (default) [#bezier-default]

Smooth cubic bezier curves — the default and most common style:

```tsx
<FlowDiagram nodes={nodes} relations={relations} pathType="bezier" />
```

Straight [#straight]

Direct straight lines between nodes:

```tsx
<FlowDiagram nodes={nodes} relations={relations} pathType="straight" />
```

Orthogonal [#orthogonal]

Right-angle polylines that follow horizontal/vertical paths only:

```tsx
<FlowDiagram nodes={nodes} relations={relations} pathType="orthogonal" />
```


# Headless Hooks (/docs/react/hooks)



Headless Hooks [#headless-hooks]

For full control, use the `useDiagram` hook directly:

```tsx
import {
  useDiagram,
  DiagramCanvas,
  DiagramNode,
  DiagramEdges,
} from '@diax/react';

function MyDiagram() {
  const {
    nodes,
    edges,
    layoutMap,
    containerProps,
    highlightedNodes,
    highlightedEdgeIds,
  } = useDiagram({
    // [!code highlight]
    nodes: [
      { id: 'a', content: 'Start' },
      { id: 'b', content: 'End' },
    ],
    relations: ['a->b'],
    highlightOnHover: true,
  });

  return (
    <DiagramCanvas {...containerProps}>
      {nodes.map((node) => (
        <DiagramNode key={node.id} {...node.bindProps}>
          {' '}
          // [!code highlight]
          {/* You own the rendering completely */}
          <div className="bg-blue-500 rounded-lg p-4 text-white">
            {node.data.content}
          </div>
        </DiagramNode>
      ))}
      <DiagramEdges
        edges={edges}
        layoutMap={layoutMap}
        highlightedNodes={highlightedNodes}
        highlightedEdgeIds={highlightedEdgeIds}
      />
    </DiagramCanvas>
  );
}
```

Advanced Composition & Reactivity [#advanced-composition--reactivity]

When bypassing the provided rendering layers entirely, spreading `node.bindProps` is essential. It guarantees your nodes opt into DiaX's built-in behavior:

1. **Grid Placement**: `data-diax-node`, `data-diax-col`, `data-diax-row` styles that tell CSS Grid where to put the item based on the core engine's layout solver.
2. **Accessibility metadata**: Binds the target DOM `id` and computes valid `aria-flowto` references. The attribute is a relationship hint; assistive technology still follows DOM order and authored semantics.
3. **Interactivity**: Binds `onMouseEnter` and `onMouseLeave` callbacks enabling the `highlightOnHover` capabilities out of the box dynamically across connected components.

Theme state [#theme-state]

Theme selection is ordinary React state. Pass the selected value to the high-level diagram and let
that module own theme resolution and CSS injection:

```tsx
import { useState } from 'react';
import { FlowDiagram, type ThemeInput } from '@diax/react';

function App() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState<ThemeInput>('linear');

  return (
    <div className="p-8">
      <button onClick={() => setTheme(theme === 'light' ? 'linear' : 'light')}>
        Toggle Theme
      </button>

      <FlowDiagram theme={theme} nodes={...} relations={...} />
    </div>
  );
}
```

Direct theme authors can import `themes`, `themeToCSS`, or `themeToStyle` from `diax/themes` without
adding a second React state abstraction.

Independent payload types [#independent-payload-types]

`useDiagram<NodeContent, EdgeLabel, GroupLabel>()` preserves separate domain types for bound nodes,
parsed edge labels, and semantic groups. Inference is preferred; pass explicit arguments only for
an empty definition or a renderer whose callback context cannot infer them. String shorthand keeps
the parsed edge-label type as `EdgeLabel | string`.

Image Export [#image-export]

`@diax/react` does not currently export a `useExport` hook. DiaX diagrams combine ordinary DOM
nodes and an SVG edge layer, so serializing only the SVG cannot preserve the complete diagram.

For now, wrap the diagram in an element you own and integrate a DOM-capture library at the
application boundary. Pin fonts, background colors and asset loading in that integration and test
the resulting image in the browsers you support. The Playground now verifies complete DOM + SVG
PNG/SVG export as an opt-in product workflow, but that implementation is not a stable framework
interface. See [Export DOM Visuals](/docs/guide/exporting).


# React Guide (/docs/react)





<InstallTabs packages="['@diax/react']" description="React bindings (peer dependency: react >= 18)" />

<Callout type="warn">
  **Next.js / SSR**: DiaX uses DOM measurement for edge rendering. In Next.js
  App Router, add `'use client'` at the top of any file that imports from
  `@diax/react`. The shell may be prerendered, while pixel edges appear after
  browser hydration and measurement. See the
  [dedicated SSR guide](/docs/react/ssr) for more details.
</Callout>

Choose the Layout Owner First [#choose-the-layout-owner-first]

| Job                  | Import                | Layout owner | Use when                                                       |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Dynamic/data Diagram | `@diax/react`         | DiaX         | Nodes and relations already exist as data                      |
| Static JSX Diagram   | `@diax/react/jsx`     | DiaX         | You are hand-authoring a visual story in TSX                   |
| Connect              | `@diax/react/connect` | Your DOM/CSS | JSX/Tailwind already owns placement and only needs connections |

These are separate loading and ownership seams. JSX authoring still becomes the same Diagram
Definition; it is not a mode switch. Optional entries are deliberately not re-exported from
`@diax/react`, so a data Diagram consumer evaluates neither the JSX extractor nor Connect runtime.

Progressive Diagram API [#progressive-diagram-api]

DiaX provides three levels of control. Choose based on your needs:

| Layer | API                              | Best for                               |
| ----- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| 1     | `<FlowDiagram>` / `<Mindmap>`    | Quick usage, AI output, prototyping    |
| 2     | `<FlowDiagram renderNode={...}>` | Custom styling with your design system |
| 3     | `useDiagram()` hook              | Full headless control, library authors |

***

Quick Start [#quick-start]

The simplest way to use DiaX — just pass nodes and relations:

```tsx contract
import { FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react';

function MyDiagram() {
  return (
    <FlowDiagram
      nodes={[
        { id: 'client', content: 'Browser' },
        { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
        { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
      ]}
      relations={['client->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db']}
      density="comfortable"
    />
  );
}
```

<DiagramPreview
  title="Quick Start — zero config"
  code="`<FlowDiagram
nodes={[
  { id: 'client', content: 'Browser' },
  { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
  { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
]}
relations={[
  'client->|HTTPS|api',
  'api->|SQL|db',
]}
density=&#x22;comfortable&#x22;
/>`"
>
  <FlowDiagram
    nodes="[
    { id: 'client', content: 'Browser' },
    { id: 'api', content: 'API Server' },
    { id: 'db', content: 'Database' },
  ]"
    relations="['client->|HTTPS|api', 'api->|SQL|db']"
    density="comfortable"
  />
</DiagramPreview>

Hand-author a static visual story [#hand-author-a-static-visual-story]

When the topology is written directly in the component rather than produced by data, use the JSX
leaf. Keep nodes and edges as siblings:

```tsx
import { DiaxEdge, DiaxNode, FlowDiagram } from '@diax/react/jsx';

<FlowDiagram>
  <DiaxNode id="brief"><BriefCard /></DiaxNode>
  <DiaxNode id="decision"><DecisionCard /></DiaxNode>
  <DiaxEdge from="brief" to="decision" label="supports" />
</FlowDiagram>
```

If `services` and `links` are already arrays, do not map them back into marker JSX. Use
`<FlowDiagram nodes={services} relations={links} />` from `@diax/react` directly. See
[JSX Authoring](/docs/react/jsx-composition) for the complete rule set.

Connect Existing JSX and Tailwind [#connect-existing-jsx-and-tailwind]

Use the dedicated leaf when the visual is primarily an authored report, comparison, code walkthrough
or application UI. Keep relations centralized and mark the exact DOM elements that should be measured:

```tsx
'use client';

import { ConnectionSurface, connectionTarget } from '@diax/react/connect';

const relations = [
  {
    from: 'brief',
    to: 'decision',
    label: <span className="rounded-full bg-indigo-600 px-2 py-1 text-white">approved</span>,
    sourceAnchor: 'right',
    targetAnchor: 'left',
  },
];

export function DecisionReport() {
  return (
    <ConnectionSurface
      relations={relations}
      className="grid gap-16 md:grid-cols-2"
      onDiagnostics={diagnostics => console.log(diagnostics)}
    >
      <section {...connectionTarget('brief')} className="rounded-2xl border p-6">
        <h3>AI brief</h3>
        <p>Ordinary semantic DOM, responsive CSS and your design system stay intact.</p>
      </section>
      <article {...connectionTarget('decision')} className="rounded-2xl bg-emerald-50 p-6">
        <h3>Decision</h3>
        <button type="button">Open evidence</button>
      </article>
    </ConnectionSurface>
  );
}
```

The nearest Surface owns the target-ID scope. A custom Target component must forward the object from
`connectionTarget(id)` to one real DOM element. Content resize, responsive reflow, images and Web
Fonts are observed automatically; there is no manual `refresh()` interface. Portals and relations
across separate Surfaces are intentionally unsupported.

See [Connect authored DOM](/docs/react/connect) for the complete API, diagnostics, constraints and
responsive composition patterns.

Inspect Runnable Diagram Studies [#inspect-runnable-diagram-studies]

These examples start from nodes and relations, then let DiaX own placement, routing and label
clearance. Open each study to compare the live DOM with its registry source.

<ShowcaseStudies slugs="['ci-pipeline', 'decision-tree', 'microservices-arch']" />

Density [#density]

Control spacing with the `density` prop:

| Value           | Description                             |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `"compact"`     | Tight spacing, good for inline diagrams |
| `"comfortable"` | Default, balanced spacing               |
| `"spacious"`    | Wide spacing, good for presentations    |

Direction [#direction]

```tsx
<FlowDiagram direction="horizontal" />         // Left to right (default)
<FlowDiagram direction="vertical" />            // Top to bottom
<FlowDiagram direction="horizontal-reverse" />  // Right to left
<FlowDiagram direction="vertical-reverse" />    // Bottom to top
```

| Value                  | Description                    |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `"horizontal"`         | Left to right (default)        |
| `"vertical"`           | Top to bottom                  |
| `"horizontal-reverse"` | Right to left (RTL flows)      |
| `"vertical-reverse"`   | Bottom to top (upstream flows) |

Layout Algorithms [#layout-algorithms]

Use the dedicated component for each layout type:

```tsx
import { FlowDiagram, Mindmap } from '@diax/react';

<FlowDiagram nodes={...} relations={...} />  // DAG layout
<Mindmap nodes={...} relations={...} />       // Center-outward radial
```

***
